articles.title: Broken Yolk Cafe Names Bodine Berger Director of Franchise Development
articles.titleKo: Broken Yolk Cafe Names Bodine Berger Director of Franchise Development
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . rior to his most recent franchise development roles with Domino's and Steak n' Shake, Bodine spent years building the footprint for another concept in the breakfast segment. Broken Yolk Cafe has appointed Bodine Berger to serve as the brand’s Director of Franchise Development. Berger will be the latest addition to a franchise sales team that’s tripled in size over the last 12 months, as the brand sets its sights on record-level development over the next three to five years. Berger has held development roles with Eggs Up Grill, Steak ‘n Shake, and Domino’s Pizza, and brings a proven track record of forward-thinking strategies that expand franchise footprints. In his role, Berger will broaden the search for franchise candidates on a national scale and support the brand’s continued coast-to-coast growth with new partners. In recent years, Broken Yolk Cafe’s franchise opportunity has expanded across Arizona, California, Idaho, Nevada, and Texas, bringing it to a systemwide total of 42 cafe locations. The franchise is also preparing to make its Midwest debut next month, after striking a multi-unit agreement for Lafayette, Indiana, earlier this year, which will bring two cafe locations to the market. “This brand has spent decades honing its people-first culture, developing an elevated and inclusive cafe experience, and, as a result, its category-leading AUV in the breakfast and brunch space,” Berger said. “I can say from firsthand experience in the breakfast segment, Broken Yolk Cafe is primed to double in size over the next several years, as the immense whitespace that exists for the brand throughout the country continues to attract new partners wanting to explore the two-daypart model.” Of particular interest to Broken Yolk Cafe’s growth plans is the continued development of its emerging market territories. This includes Boise, Dallas, Indianapolis, Northern California, and Phoenix. “With franchise development, our focus has always been on quality over quantity,” said John Gelastopoulos, CEO of Broken Yolk Cafe. “While Bodine’s addition to the team won’t alter that approach, his experience is sure to accelerate our expansion into new markets and communities nationwide.” Broken Yolk Cafe is currently seeking experienced operators to help drive the brand’s expansion, and is offering franchise owners a 2.5% royalty reduction for years 1 and 2 on all stores under an area development agreement signed before March 31, 2027. articles.title: Logan’s Roadhouse Announces Comfort Food Lineup for Fall Season
articles.titleKo: Logan’s Roadhouse Announces Comfort Food Lineup for Fall Season
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Slow-roasted Prime Rib is making its fall comeback at Logan’s Roadhouse, and it’s bringing a fresh lineup of comfort food favorites along for the ride. The Original Roadhouse is welcoming the season with Fireside Favorites, a limited-time menu featuring Lemon Caper Fried Chicken, Honey BBQ Pork Chops and an Apple Pie Cookie Ice Cream Sandwich made with warm apple-filled cookies, vanilla ice cream and caramel. For holiday gatherings, Logan’s is also bringing back Prime Rib as an option in its Ultimate Roadhouse Feast, available hot-and-ready or take-and-bake. “Fall is a great time to play with richer flavors and comfort-food,” said Chef Luis Haro, VP of Culinary Innovation for Logan’s Roadhouse. “Cajun butter spread and a roasted jalapeño bring some heat to our Texas Ribeye, while apple and roasted corn compote adds a little sweetness to our Honey BBQ Pork Chops. Sometimes a small change in flavor is all it takes to make a familiar favorite feel new again.” Fireside Favorites: Fall Comfort Food With a Roadhouse Kick Arrives Oct. 26 The limited-time lineup includes: Texas Ribeye: A 12-oz. hand-cut ribeye topped with Cajun butter and a roasted jalapeño, served with two sides. Honey BBQ Pork Chops: Two 6-oz. pork chops glazed with Honey BBQ sauce and served over apple and corn compote, with two sides. Lemon Caper Fried Chicken: Hand-breaded chicken breast smothered in lemon caper sauce and served over mashed potatoes, with two sides. Shrimp Scampi Pasta: Barilla Al Bronzo linguine topped with six jumbo shrimp, broccoli, creamy scampi sauce and Parmesan cheese, served with cheesy bread. Also available with an 8-oz. hand-cut salmon fillet. 8-oz. Sirloin & Shrimp Scampi: Mesquite wood-grilled sirloin topped with three jumbo shrimp prepared scampi style, served with two sides. Guests can also add scampi-style shrimp to any steak. Appetizers include Classic Shrimp Cocktail and hot Spin Dip with tortilla chips. Fireside Fixin’s, available à la carte, include Double Baked Potato, Grilled Zucchini, Creamed Corn and Wedge Salad. For dessert, Logan’s is putting a new spin on apple pie à la mode with its Apple Pie Cookie Ice Cream Sandwich. Two warm, apple-filled cookies sandwich vanilla ice cream, finished with caramel and whipped cream. Seasonal cocktails include the Mango Rancher ’Rita, made with Casamigos Blanco Tequila, Grand Marnier, mango and Key lime flavors; an Old Fashioned with Elijah Craig Bourbon; and the Original Roadhouse Tea, Logan’s take on a Long Island Iced Tea. Prime Rib Weekends Return Oct. 30 Beginning Friday, Oct. 30, Logan’s 13-oz. Prime Rib will be available every Friday through Sunday while supplies last. Seasoned with Logan’s signature rub, slow-roasted for six hours and hand-carved to order, each cut is served with a choice of two sides. Bring the Roadhouse Home for the Holidays Holiday hosts can leave the cooking to Logan’s with the Ultimate Roadhouse Feasts, available hot-and-ready or take-and-bake. Serving six to eight people, each feast includes a choice of Fall-Off-The-Bone Ribs, Meatloaf or Pork Chops, with Prime Rib available as a seasonal option, plus one dozen of Logan’s signature yeast rolls, a house salad, two sides and dessert. Preorders open Oct. 30 for pickup Nov. 20 through Jan. 1, with orders required at least 24 hours in advance. Logan’s is also offering a holiday gift card promotion from Nov. 16 through Dec. 31. Guests who purchase $50 in gift cards will receive a free $10 bonus card. Bonus cards are redeemable Nov. 17 through Feb. 11 and not redeemable the same day of purchase. To learn more or find a participating restaurant, visit LogansRoadhouse.com. Menu items, pricing and participation may vary by location. Must be 21 or older to purchase alcoholic beverages. articles.title: Can Rom Krupp’s Latest Innovation Get Hospitality Back Into Casual Dining?
articles.titleKo: Can Rom Krupp’s Latest Innovation Get Hospitality Back Into Casual Dining?
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Rom Krupp has a background in sociology and economics. But it’s not a muscle he’s flexed all that much over the past three decades in technology. If there ever was a time to change that, though, it was 20 or so months ago when it became clear to Krupp consumers were asking for hospitality in an ever-transactional dining space, with prices failing to match experience. And that’s a debate that often starts with churn, a hardly a new conversation in full-service dining. Per the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, there are roughly 2.3 million servers clocking in each year. And somewhere around 423,000 positions in need of being filled. The National Restaurant Association tabs server turnaround at 89 percent and a Cornell study figured the replacement cost for each employee at $5,800. Average retention? About 110 days, according to 7shifts. Krupp, who leads his company OneDine, spoke with about a dozen CEOs and asked them how they’re addressing the age-old issue of knowledge vacating the building when an employee does. Most replied with a stock, “we’re working on retention.” Krupp saw a different reality. Retention, he feels, is a privilege of restaurants with higher per person averages. Unless you’re in a small market where a lower PPA is, relatively speaking, lofty, your best servers are going to elevate out of the role or head to restaurants where they can wait on larger checks. “So,” Krupp said, “retention is not the answer.” “And that’s where I got a bit of insight—they’re all trying to fix retention. The problem is that you can’t.” Rather, what operators need to address, he says, is the cost of churn; not churn itself. This, too, wasn’t novel. Only it’s historically been accepted as a “cost of business.” It’s a mammoth estimate of $5 billion of costs flowing out the door for an industry where, per February data from the Association, 42 percent of restaurants failed to turn a profit last year and average net profit was 3.6 percent. “At the end of the day, you can build the best technology in the world,” Krupp says. “If servers don’t want to use it, you’re not going to be able to implement it successfully. … How do you align everybody on the same goal? Well, you’ve got to give them a tool they want to use. You give them a tool that makes the guest experience better.” And so, Krupp took a hard look at handheld tablets and what’s happening at the table. Back to some sociology “The problem today,” Krupp says, “is we hire servers almost like we hire flight attendants.” What he’s illustrating is an experience you’ve likely encountered. Airlines give attendants a primary task of safety. They’re on the plane to get customers from Point A to Point B and people are conditioned to forgive what happens in between. Has the same begun to happen in full service? If a server’s No. 1 target is to take orders, great service becomes a bonus. “The reality is, we spend so much time ramping them up to be great order takers that we neglect to make them great hosts,” Krupp says. “And they’re hosting a party. They’re hosting an experience.” His point is, don’t eliminate training; stop training servers on the process of order taking and instead train them on delivering hospitality. It sounds elementary but it’s hardly easy to execute, particularly with the earlier notion around churn. What Krupp set out to build addresses this ideal—allow operators to teach servers to be great hosts while letting technology take care of the order asking knowledge. “All the billions of dollars in execution falls down to the one person you’re interacting with on the flight,” he says of the airline example. “Then, it happens to restaurants.” For the past 20 months, Krupp’s team worked on a solution called “Restaurant Ordering Mentor,” or ROM, fittingly. The two longtime business partners will be recognized at the Georgia Restaurant Association Crystal of Excellence (GRACE) Awards Gala on Monday, December 7, 2026, for their outstanding careers and lasting contributions to Georgia’s restaurant and hospitality industry. For more than three decades, Saxe and Aaron have shaped Atlanta’s restaurant community, transforming a small neighborhood bagel shop into a thriving, diversified company with operations spanning restaurants, food manufacturing, and aviation food service. Under their leadership, Goldbergs has expanded well beyond its restaurant operations into catering, food manufacturing, and aviation food service, all while maintaining the quality, consistency, and customer service that built its reputation. Their success reflects not only their ability to recognize new business opportunities, but also their commitment to creating jobs, providing long-term career opportunities, and building a company that has become a familiar part of Atlanta families’ lives. Their story began in Johannesburg, South Africa, where both men entered the restaurant industry through different paths. Saxe was working as an accountant when an opportunity to invest in a struggling restaurant led him to discover his passion for the business. Aaron began working in restaurants in 1972, learning the industry from the ground up before eventually opening his own establishment. Their paths crossed when Aaron became a meat supplier for Saxe’s restaurant, and what began as a professional relationship developed into a lasting friendship, family connection, and business partnership. Sharing similar values and a desire to build something of their own, they eventually decided to relocate to the United States and pursue new opportunities. In 1992, Saxe and Aaron acquired Goldberg & Son, a small Atlanta bagel business that would become the foundation of their future success. Through years of hard work, careful expansion, and a commitment to serving quality food, they established Goldbergs Fine Foods as a respected name in Atlanta’s restaurant community. As the company grew, they kept looking for ways to improve operations, expand their offerings, and reach new customers without losing the neighborhood atmosphere and personal service that made Goldbergs successful. Today, the restaurants remain a gathering place for generations of Atlanta families, many of whom have been customers for decades. Saxe’s entrepreneurial vision has driven the company’s expansion beyond traditional restaurant operations. Recognizing the importance of controlling product quality and consistency, he began producing food in-house from a small kitchen at Goldbergs’ West Paces Ferry location. What started with deli favorites such as tuna salad, chicken salad, and other products eventually grew into the company’s broader food manufacturing capabilities. This approach created opportunities to serve customers through new business channels, including aviation food service. It helped establish Goldbergs Group as a diversified food and hospitality enterprise serving customers both in restaurants and through broader aviation and food service channels. Equally important to the company’s success has been Aaron’s focus on its employees and customers. Having worked in nearly every aspect of restaurant operations throughout his career, Aaron believes that successful leadership begins with understanding the people who make a business run. articles.title: Landry’s and TREW Capital to Acquire Fireman Group Restaurants in $22 Million Deal
articles.titleKo: Landry’s and TREW Capital to Acquire Fireman Group Restaurants in $22 Million Deal
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Landry's is expected to own and operate Bond 45, Café Fiorello, and Trattoria Dell'Arte. TREW Capital will take over Paris Bar, Le Jardin, Café Paradiso, Brooklyn Diner, and Brooklyn Delicatessen. Landry’s and TREW Capital Management are preparing to take ownership of several prominent New York City restaurants following a bankruptcy auction that resulted in a $22.2 million deal for The Fireman Group’s restaurant assets. The transaction received approval Thursday, clearing a major hurdle in the sale of restaurants including Bond 45, Café Fiorello, Trattoria Dell’Arte, Brooklyn Diner, and Paris Bar. According to court documents, Landry’s is expected to own and operate Bond 45, Café Fiorello, and Trattoria Dell’Arte. TREW Capital will take over Paris Bar, Le Jardin, Café Paradiso, Brooklyn Diner, and Brooklyn Delicatessen. Landry’s, owned by billionaire Tilman Fertitta, operates hundreds of restaurants across the country, including Morton’s The Steakhouse, Mastro’s Steakhouse, Del Frisco’s, The Palm, and McCormick & Schmick’s. TREW Capital specializes in acquiring and revitalizing distressed hospitality businesses. According to court documents, the firm operates approximately 80 restaurants employing more than 2,000 people. Its investment history includes BurgerFi, Rubio’s Coastal Grill, Bar Louie, Anthony’s Coal Fired Pizza & Wings, and Iron Hill Brewery & Restaurant. The acquisition offers a path forward for The Fireman Group, whose restaurants have been fixtures in New York City’s dining scene for decades. The company filed for bankruptcy protection in August , less than a year after the death of founder Sheldon “Shelly” Fireman. He opened The Hip Bagel in Greenwich Village in 1963 and spent the following decades building a portfolio of restaurants near some of the city’s best-known cultural destinations. Café Fiorello has operated for more than 50 years, Trattoria Dell’Arte for nearly 40, and Brooklyn Diner for roughly three decades. The restaurant group’s financial troubles stretched back several years, beginning with debt tied to construction projects and losses associated with a restaurant fire. The pandemic compounded those challenges as Broadway closures, declining tourism, and reduced Midtown office traffic hurt sales. The company later turned to merchant cash advances to cover operating expenses, creating additional financial pressure as repayments accumulated. The situation deteriorated further when disputes with certain lenders resulted in credit-card processors withholding millions of dollars in restaurant revenue. The company had less than $100,000 in available cash when it filed for bankruptcy. The Fireman Group’s financial troubles created uncertainty surrounding the future of its restaurants and more than 800 employees. Court documents indicate the business was operating at a loss and had enough available liquidity to continue operating only through the end of October. Landry’s initially submitted an offer of $9.5 million. Its original proposal focused on acquiring Café Fiorello, Trattoria Dell’Arte, and Bond 45 before expanding to additional restaurant assets. The competing bid came from FHGRF LLC, a lender to the bankrupt company. Court documents indicate that Fireman Group CEO Benjamin Grossman owned a 35.8 percent interest in FHGRF, which proposed a transaction that would have allowed him to continue serving as CEO. Following the unsuccessful bid, court documents indicate Grossman is not expected to receive an offer to continue working for the business after the acquisition. Certain other officers and employees have received, or are expected to receive, employment offers from the new owners. The work started well before the meat reached restaurant kitchens. Outback collaborated with butchers, farmers, and ranchers to improve sourcing and tighten specifications. Greater attention to trimming helps ensure guests receive the cuts and portions they ordered. Chef Efrem Cutler, Outback’s newly appointed chief steak officer, has worked with the chain for 18 years. He says the improvements came from examining the details of steak preparation, including the cooking equipment and seasonings used to bring out the characteristics of individual cuts. “You can have a great meal. The cooking method offers a contrast to the chain’s traditional seasoned-and-seared preparation on a flat-top grill. Puerto Cocina, the Mexican, Baja-inspired coastal restaurant in Dallas’ Design District, introduces weekend brunch and a new weekday happy hour. Influenced by the cuisine of Valle de Guadalupe, Baja California, Puerto Cocina’s culinary program celebrates coastal flavors with a focus on fresh seafood, a raw bar featuring crudos and tiraditos, house-made masa crisps and an emphasis on shellfish and caviar. Building on this distinctive approach, the restaurant’s new weekend brunch, available Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., features Mexican-inspired brunch favorites, fresh seafood and savory dishes, while happy hour, offered Tuesday through Friday from 5–7 p.m. exclusively in the bar lounge, introduces curated pairings of creative cocktails and flavorful bites for just $16 each. Puerto Cocina’s new weekend brunch offers a menu that balances classic brunch favorites with bold, unexpected flavors. Guests can enjoy dishes like Steak & Eggs – grilled bavette, potato hash, over-easy eggs and salsa tatemada; Chilaquiles – choice of chicken, shrimp or filet, topped with Monterey cheese, red or green salsa, pickled red onion, fried egg and crispy nopales; and Banana Bread French Toast – banana brûlée, pastry cream and café de olla syrup. For a lighter option, the Chia Seed Pudding combines strawberry jam, coconut-chia pudding, matcha, toasted coconut and pepitas. In addition to the brunch specialties, guests can enjoy a variety of dishes from Puerto Cocina’s menu during brunch, including fresh seafood, tacos, tortas and salads. Standouts include the Baja Taco with tempura-battered fish, cabbage and serrano confit slaw; Aguachile de Atun – Aguachile negro, pearl onions, jicama and candied jamaica; Milanesa Torta – chicken milanesa, cabbage slaw, serrano confit, jalapeno crema, avocado, chiltepin aioli and cotija; and Burrata Salad – figs, beets, Cara Cara oranges, candied pepitas, charred cebollita dressing and mustard frill. Puerto Cocina is also introducing a new happy hour, available Tuesday through Friday from 5–7 p.m. exclusively in the bar lounge. The menu features Curated Bocado Pairings for $16 each – thoughtfully combining a signature cocktail with a bite for an elevated and unique take on the traditional happy hour experience. Guests can choose from four distinctive pairings: Mussel Aguachile & Spritz: Confit mussels with coconut curry aguachile paired with a spritz featuring damiana, strawberry and sparkling rosé. Crab Cake & Margarita: Crab cake with anchovy aioli and salsa pelirroja paired with a margarita featuring matcha, yuzu and tequila. Butter Braised Scallop & Milk Punch: A butter-braised scallop with mignonette butter, pasilla and smoked trout roe paired with a milk punch featuring guava, mezcal and charred sourdough. Fried Oyster & Negroni: A masa-crusted oyster with pistachio salsa macha paired with a Negroni featuring melon, Salers aperitif and gin. Each pairing is designed to showcase the interplay between Puerto Cocina’s seafood-forward culinary program and creative cocktail offerings, giving guests an opportunity to experience the restaurant’s distinctive flavors in an approachable format. articles.title: Home Run Inn Launches Largest TV Campaign in its 103-Year History
articles.titleKo: Home Run Inn Launches Largest TV Campaign in its 103-Year History
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Home Run Inn Pizza, the iconic Chicago pizza brand known for bringing its tavern-style pizza from its restaurants to freezer aisles across the country, is launching a new integrated marketing campaign to drive awareness and demand for its growing CPG offering in key markets nationwide. The campaign is led by a set of new television commercials that tell the unique family owned, tavern-to-table story that makes Home Run Inn Pizza a standout in the frozen pizza category. The spots feature award-winning blues guitarist, singer/songwriter, and legend, “Billy Blues” Fruteland Jackson, further bringing the brand’s Chicago heritage to life. The campaign represents the single largest television investment in Home Run Inn’s 103-year history. The creative will begin airing in select markets nationwide in late October to coincide with National Tavern-Style Pizza Day on October 22. Online and connected video, streaming audio, out-of-home, and display advertising will support the television campaign. Home Run Inn Pizza has been serving its signature tavern-style pizza in Chicago for more than 75 years and today operates six pizzerias throughout Chicagoland. In the late 1950s, the family began par-baking and freezing those same pizzas for customers and local grocery stores, laying the foundation for a frozen pizza business that now reaches consumers nationwide. For Home Run Inn and quench, the new campaign taps into something few frozen pizza brands can claim: a product with a generational restaurant legacy behind it. “We know we have a great product and a story that resonates with consumers. The opportunity now is making sure more people know about it as we expand into new markets,” said Home Run Inn Pizza CEO Dan Costello. “This campaign is about getting our name in front of more people and sharing what makes our pizza special.” “A lot of brands can sell frozen pizza. Home Run Inn delivers a genuine Chicago pizza experience,” said quench CEO Michael Pavone. “That story is real and it’s authentic. It also gives us something powerful to work with creatively. Our job is to turn that authenticity into something that gets attention and drives sales.” The new television work is part of Home Run Inn Pizza’s ongoing efforts to introduce its signature tavern-style pizza to more consumers and build the brand in markets across the country. The nine-year maturation was chosen as a direct reference to the shirt number synonymous with Rush’s career, creating a natural connection between the whisky and one of football’s most famous number nines. But while the whisky’s name draws directly from football, its striking presentation takes its inspiration from somewhere else entirely. NINE is presented in a distinctive bottle with a gold finish, its design inspired by the sophistication, glamour and cinematic style. The pack is designed by threebrand based in Leith, Edinburgh. The result is a whisky that celebrates Rush’s footballing legacy without simply reproducing the traditional colours associated with his career. “I wore the number nine for Liverpool and it means everything to me, so this had to be nine, nine years old and named after the shirt,” said Ian Rush. “I’m a proud Welshman and Penderyn is Wales’ whisky, so there was never any other distillery I wanted to do this with. articles.title: National Restaurant Association Launches Latest Evolution of Kids LiveWell Program
articles.titleKo: National Restaurant Association Launches Latest Evolution of Kids LiveWell Program
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Finding delicious, balanced meals for children just got a little easier at thousands of restaurants across the country. Today, the National Restaurant Association launched the latest evolution of the award-winning Kids LiveWell program, a new website that helps families find restaurants offering balanced menu options for children that have been dietitian-verified to meet the program’s science-based nutrition criteria. Parents and caregivers can now easily go online and search for a restaurant near them that has committed to offering a selection of menu items for children that focus on real foods like fruits, vegetables, meat or meat alternatives, whole grains, and dairy. What is the Kids LiveWell program? Kids LiveWell is a voluntary restaurant industry program that certifies kids’ menu items against specific criteria. Registered dietitians verify each item based on menu and nutrition information provided by participating restaurants. To participate, restaurants must offer at least two meals and two sides that meet science-based nutrition criteria and include at least two food groups. Dietitians evaluate each item for calories, saturated fat, trans fat, added sugars, sodium and servings of key food groups, including fruits, vegetables, dairy, meat or meat alternatives, and whole grains. Participating restaurants must also maintain default kids’ menu beverage options of water, milk, or 100% fruit or vegetable juice. The long-standing program is the centerpiece of the restaurant industry’s commitment to providing better-for-you choices, especially for children. “Restaurants that offer Kids LiveWell-certified menu options are helping families find meals they can choose with confidence,” said Michelle Korsmo, President & CEO of the National Restaurant Association. “This new website, with an expanded roster of participating brands, makes it easier for parents and caregivers to find restaurant options that meet their family’s needs when dining out.” How does the new Kids LiveWell website work? The new Kids LiveWell website will be a trusted go-to resource for families that illustrates the program’s nutrition requirements and showcases participating brands. Parents can go to the mobile-ready site, kidslivewell.com , and click on the Good Food Finder at the top of the page to see a list of participating restaurants. To explore Kids LiveWell offerings at participating restaurants, simply click the logo to view approved meals. Parents can find an overview of the Kids LiveWell nutrition requirements at the top of the participating restaurants page on kidslivewell.com and can take an in-depth look at the nutrition criteria in the Kids LiveWell white paper here . “The new Kids LiveWell website is another way restaurants are delivering value to the families they serve, including their youngest guests,” said Korsmo. “Dining out remains an important part of daily life and families are paying closer attention to what they order and the value they receive. Paired with this new digital tool, Kids LiveWell menu options help participating operators strengthen their value proposition and meet the needs of today’s consumers.” Which restaurants participate in Kids LiveWell? Kids LiveWell restaurants fit the needs of every family’s lifestyle. Menu options are available across quickservice, fast casual, and fullservice restaurants, including both independent operators and national chains. Regardless of restaurant type, all participants must meet the same rigorous nutrition standards, which are independently verified by third-party dietitians. articles.title: Cuisine Cuisine at The Mira Welcomes Newly Appointed Chinese Executive Chef Lau Sze‑yau, Presenting Cantonese Cuisine Reimagined Through Craft, Heritage and Memory
articles.titleKo: Cuisine Cuisine at The Mira Welcomes Newly Appointed Chinese Executive Chef Lau Sze‑yau, Presenting Cantonese Cuisine Reimagined Through Craft, Heritage and Memory
articles.originalSummary: Michelin-recommended contemporary Cantonese restaurant Cuisine Cuisine at The Mira , Tsim Sha Tsui, welcomes Lau Sze-yau as its new Executive Chef. An award-winning master of Cantonese cuisine whose distinguished career has seen him helm some of the city’s most respected Chinese dining establishments, Chef Lau brings a fresh perspective, two decades of experience and vibrant energy to the kitchen. Blending both innovation and tradition, his core culinary philosophy is grounded in three essential chapters – craft, heritage and memory – that unite to expand the possibilities and showcase the evolution of Cantonese cuisine. These fundamentals underpin a newly unveiled à la carte menu which retains signature classics for convivial celebrations, reimagines family favourites with nostalgic warmth, and introduces inventive creations that heighten the excitement of fine Chinese dining. Uniting Chef Lau’s culinary ingenuity with modern aesthetics in the restaurant’s elegant setting, the menu presents an exquisite feast designed to engage all the senses. With over two decades of culinary experience, Executive Chef Lau Sze-yau’s gastronomic journey was first sparked in childhood during family reunion dinners. Watching elders transform simple, fresh ingredients into a banquet of rich flavours – and seeing the joy it brought to loved ones – deeply moved him. This early realisation that delicious food brings happiness and nostalgia nourishes the soul ignited his lifelong passion for cooking. Chef Lau’s career in Cantonese gastronomy spans leading hospitality brands including The Hong Kong Bankers Club, Hong Kong Parkview and the Clearwater Bay Golf & Country Club. He honed his expertise at the Chinese Culinary Institute under the Vocational Training Council, completing advanced master classes and the Master Chef Course in Chinese Cuisine, where he was honoured as Outstanding Trainee of the 10th programme. His talent has earned widespread industry recognition, with consecutive gold and silver awards at the Vocational Training Council’s Asian Culinary Exchange from 2017 to 2019. Dedicated to promoting Cantonese culinary culture, he serves on the committees of the Asia Art of Cuisine Society and the Hong Kong Chinese Chefs Association, and was a judge at the 2019 Hong Kong International Culinary Classic. I am thrilled to join Cuisine Cuisine at The Mira and to share my contemporary vision of Cantonese cuisine, conceived through craft, heritage and memory, with multi-generational families of Hong Kong gourmands and guests from around the world,” says Executive Chef Lau Sze‑yau. “Grounded in authentic Cantonese flavours, my creations are elevated with modern touches in refined and often surprising presentations, ingredient pairings and culinary techniques. In harmony with the restaurant’s elegant concept, my goal is to curate memorable dining journeys that captivate through taste, aroma and visual beauty. Under the leadership of Chef Lau, Cuisine Cuisine at The Mira unveils nine new signature creations spanning appetisers, main courses and desserts – each testament to his versatility and creativity. This flavour journey unfolds across three chapters: infusing dynamic new life into traditional Cantonese frameworks, honouring time‑tested craftsmanship, and evoking cherished memories at the table. Guests are invited to immerse themselves in the chef’s storybook of tastes, savouring the heritage of Chinese culture while reconnecting with “the joy of memory” – nostalgic moments when flavour, love and happiness intertwined around the family table. Chapter I – Creative Artistry Premium ingredients, handpicked for quality and seasonality, are reimagined through refined techniques, inventive flavour pairings and contemporary presentation. Classic Cantonese dining is elevated into discoveries, where precision and artistry reveal fresh dimensions of taste. articles.title: Texas-Based Hotel Thompson Austin Taps Sergio Ledesma to Lead Rooftop Restaurant
articles.titleKo: Texas-Based Hotel Thompson Austin Taps Sergio Ledesma to Lead Rooftop Restaurant
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Thompson Austin and tommie Austin are pleased to announce the appointment of Sergio Ledesma as executive chef of Arriba Abajo Rooftop Cantina, the hotels’ signature rooftop restaurant. Located on the fourth floor of Thompson Austin, just steps from the city’s famed Sixth Street, Arriba Abajo pairs sweeping views of the downtown skyline with vibrant Mexican cuisine inspired by the flavors of Oaxaca, Yucatán and Tulum. Originally from Mexico, Ledesma brings a deep appreciation for Mexican culinary traditions, ingredients and hospitality to Arriba Abajo, shaped by a career spanning acclaimed restaurants and hotels. After studying at The Culinary Institute of America, he went on to serve as executive chef at La Central San Pedro, an upscale steakhouse in San Pedro Garza García, Mexico, before making his way to Austin, where he most recently led the culinary program at Hotel Van Zandt, a boutique hotel in the heart of downtown and home to the acclaimed restaurant Geraldine’s. “Having spent the last several years in Austin, I’ve built a deep appreciation for this city and its incredible culinary community,” said Ledesma. “What excites me about Arriba Abajo is the opportunity to bring the flavors and traditions I grew up with in Mexico to our guests and share them in a way that feels genuine and approachable. I’m looking forward to working with the team, continuing to learn and creating a place where people can come together and enjoy great food.” At Arriba Abajo, Ledesma will draw on his Mexican roots and years of culinary expertise to further shape the restaurant’s menu, emphasizing bold flavors, seasonal ingredients and thoughtful technique. Inspired by the family meals and food traditions of his childhood, his approach reflects a belief that great dining goes beyond the plate, bringing people together through food, storytelling and a shared sense of hospitality. Ledesma also brings fresh energy to Arriba Abajo’s hidden mezcalería, También, with a reimagined take on its multisensory, multi-course tasting, Mezcal, También. Available exclusively on November 12 and 19, a new seven-course experience will celebrate Mexico’s culinary diversity, with each course highlighting the cuisine of one of the country’s seven regions. The program will continue with specialty holiday lineups throughout December before transitioning in 2027 to monthly rotating menus, each dedicated to the culinary traditions of a different Mexican region. articles.title: Ted’s Montana Grill to Close Locations on Thanksgiving and Christmas
articles.titleKo: Ted’s Montana Grill to Close Locations on Thanksgiving and Christmas
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Ted’s Montana Grill, the classic American grill known for elevated, timeless cuisine with bold flavors and fresh, authentic ingredients, has announced that all locations will close annually on Thanksgiving Day and Christmas Day so the team can celebrate with the people who matter most. “We’re grateful for our passionate, dedicated team, who give their best year-round and bring what we call the ‘Big Sky Spirit’ to life every day,” said George McKerrow, CEO and co-founder of Ted’s Montana Grill. “A spirited culture is built on the belief that the best guest experiences start from a team that feels supported and valued. Thanksgiving has been one of our biggest sales days, but family comes first, and giving our team time with loved ones is one way we show our appreciation.” Ted’s commitment to its team comes during a year of positive momentum. Guest ratings on Yelp and Google have increased for four consecutive years. Internal management survey results also underscore the strength and engagement of Ted’s leadership team, with 100% participation and an impressive score of 3.97 out of 4, reflecting strong confidence in the Ted’s Montana Grill concept. The spirit of the season will extend beyond Ted’s own team too. Ted’s Montana Grill will host special holiday dinners for families facing hardship, offering a welcoming place to gather, share a heartwarming meal, and experience the warmth of genuine hospitality. Community members are invited to nominate families who have faced challenges or demonstrated extraordinary strength, kindness or generosity. Ted’s is also renewing its commitment to an exceptional dining experience. Every single team member will receive refreshed training on delivering the ‘Big Sky Spirit’ at every step of the guest journey. This includes comprehensive steak training, preparing feel-good, high-quality meals in-house with no microwaves or freezers, and treating every guest like family in their own home. “Our people are at the heart of everything we do, and every guest deserves to feel that from the moment they walk through our doors,” said Ted’s Montana Grill President Kristi Martin. “The Big Sky Spirit is about more than great food. It’s about genuine hospitality, attention to every detail, and doing things the right way, with no shortcuts. We’re committed to delivering a best-in-class experience every time, serving real food for real people, and making every guest feel like part of the family.” HELP US SHARE THE SPIRIT OF THE SEASON. HERE’S HOW TO NOMINATE A FAMILY: The community is invited to nominate a family who has experienced hardships or shown exceptional kindness and generosity toward others. Share their story and why they deserve a special holiday dinner at Ted’s Montana Grill. Email bigskyspirit@tedsmontanagrill.com by Nov. 11, 2026. Please include the full name of the nominee and their contact information. The post Ted’s Montana Grill to Close Locations on Thanksgiving and Christmas appeared first on FSR magazine .

articles.title: OneDine Introduces Conversational Tableside Ordering Technology
articles.titleKo: OneDine Introduces Conversational Tableside Ordering Technology
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Restaurant operators have spent decades trying to solve one of the industry’s most persistent problems: every time a server leaves, valuable knowledge leaves with them. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, there are approximately 2.3 million servers working in restaurants today, yet every year more than 423,000 positions must be filled, creating a continuous cycle of onboarding, training, and knowledge loss. Today, OneDine launched Restaurant Ordering Mentor (ROM™), a patent-pending, POS-agnostic server intelligence platform built to address one of the restaurant industry’s largest hidden profit drains: workforce churn. As operators face constant recruiting, onboarding and retraining cycles, ROM puts the intelligence of the restaurant directly into the hands of every server, reducing dependence on menu memorization, accelerating productivity, improving consistency, and freeing teams to focus on hospitality. For operators, that means faster ramp-up and stronger execution. For restaurant executives, it means increasing profitability in an industry where turnover remains a constant challenge. Instead of memorizing where modifiers live, learning menu structures, and searching through screens while standing at the table, ROM allows servers to enter orders with just a few keystrokes, as if they’re texting on a phone. ROM quickly and intuitively interprets even just a couple of letters, mapping to any restaurant’s menu data and guides servers along the ordering flow, ensuring every order is placed accurately, aligned with the brand’s business goals, like required selections, dietary accommodations, and even preferred pairings and upsells. The result is faster onboarding, greater consistency, improved productivity and more time for servers to focus on true hospitality. “The future of restaurant technology isn’t about replacing people. It’s about helping people perform at their best,” commented Mike Axiotis, President and CEO, Lehigh Valley Restaurant Brands and Chair, National Restaurant Association Board of Directors. “For decades, our industry has invested heavily in systems that improve transactions and operations. The next frontier is helping frontline teams deliver better hospitality. That’s why innovations like ROM are so interesting. They represent a shift toward technology that strengthens the human side of restaurants rather than competing with it.” “For more than 30 years, we’ve asked servers to adapt to technology that was never designed for the way they actually work,” said Rom Krupp, Founder and CEO of OneDine. “We train them to memorize menus, learn modifier paths, navigate screens, and master complex systems before they can fully focus on the guest. ROM turns that model on its head. Instead of forcing people to think like the POS, ROM allows technology to work the way people naturally communicate. We believe that’s one of the most significant changes to tableside ordering since the POS was introduced.” After 20 months of intense R&D, field testing and validation, ROM is available immediately for full-service restaurant deployments. Competing on a show like Top Chef looks a lot like living inside a pressure cooker—and there are pros and cons to that, as one can imagine. The high-pressure environment is stressful, and forces chefs to quickly learn and adapt to survive. But they come out on the other end irrevocably changed in one way or another—whether it’s the practical lesson of knowing exactly what you can execute in 30 minutes, the reality of what national exposure does (and doesn’t) do for reservations, or the emotional shift that comes from turning a cast of competitors into a kind of restaurant-family for life. Charbel Hayek ( Top Chef Middle East & North Africa (MENA) Season 5 and Top Chef: World All-Stars ) puts it best: “The pressure will push you to move faster and make decisions in seconds, but you still need to trust your instincts, taste your food, and remember why you’re competing.” Across five former “cheftestants,” a few recurring themes emerged: the shift from solo talent to shared leadership and real teamwork, and the way that living under the clock sharpened their instincts, clarified their point of view, and taught them to treat every dish and every decision as intentional. In the stories and interviews that follow, they explain where Top Chef pushed them, what stuck, and how those lessons are shaping their decision-making today. What lingers in the end is a new way of thinking about food, leadership, and what it actually takes to run a restaurant in 2026. Even before competing on the most recent season of Top Chef: Carolinas in Charlotte, which premiered in March 2026, Jones received a national recognition that many chefs only dream of. Back in late January, he remembers exercising in the gym at work when a friend texted him, “Congrats on the nom,” to which Jones replied, “What are you talking about?” His friend told him to go check Instagram—and that’s how Jones found out he was named a 2026 James Beard Award semifinalist for Emerging Chef. He stepped out of the room, feeling emotional. “That was a groundbreaking moment for me,” he says. “I will say, the gym is not the right place to shed tears. It makes everyone in the room with you feel a little uncomfortable,” he laughs. “So I had to pop out of there real quick. But I was beyond happy.” Before filming season 23 of Top Chef, Jones was helping celebrity chef Marcus Samuelsson launch Marcus DC inside The Morrow Hotel, which officially opened in D.C.’s Union Market District on June 3, 2025. Samuelsson tapped Jones to lead the kitchen as executive chef, where he has crafted a menu that reflects his upbringing in nearby Sunderland, Maryland, close to Chesapeake Bay. Mel’s Crab Rice, a mainstay on the Marcus DC menu, is a great example. Jones grew up cracking crabs with his family, and turned that childhood memory into one of DC’s most sought-after dishes: a mix of crunchy shallots, okra, obe, and uni-infused béarnaise. articles.titleKo: Tom’s Watch Bar Names Shannon McNiel CEO
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Tom’s Watch Bar, the ultimate destination for sports viewing and entertainment, today announced the appointment of Shannon McNiel as Chief Executive Officer, effective immediately. McNiel, previously co-CEO and an experienced operator who has led the brand since November 2024 in close partnership with co-CEO Brooks Schaden, will now lead a critical stage of growth for Tom’s Watch Bar as the brand continues to evolve and strengthen its position as a leading concept in the consumer entertainment and sports experience category. Brooks Schaden will return to his role as CEO at SIF Partners, the investment firm that owns Tom’s Watch Bar, and will continue to support the brand as a member of the Board of Directors and ownership group. Rick Schaden will remain as Executive Chairman. “Over the last decade, Tom’s Watch Bar has grown into a profitable entertainment and experience concept with venues in major cities across the U.S. and with fans around the world,” said Rick Schaden, Executive Chairman of Tom’s Watch Bar’s Board of Directors. “I’ve worked with Shannon for many years and have deep faith in his ability to develop great teams and deliver results, and I believe he is the right person to lead Tom’s Watch Bar as it becomes the next growth leader in consumer entertainment and sports. I look forward to continuing to partner with Brooks as a member of our Board, where his experience will continue to be invaluable in shaping the direction of the Company.” Since 2014, McNiel has played an instrumental role in building Tom’s Watch Bar into a successful multi-unit brand. He previously served as the company’s Chief Operating Officer and has decades of senior leadership experience from several well-known restaurants, including Texas Roadhouse, Bubba’s 33, Cheddar’s Scratch Kitchen, and Darden. “I’m proud to have been a part of this brand since it first began and look forward to taking this great brand into its next chapter,” said Shannon McNiel. “My vision is for us to transform Tom’s Watch Bar into the most recognized sports viewing and fan engagement brand in America, and I look forward to working with our incredible team to make that dream a reality as we extend into new markets across the country.” Tom’s Watch Bar has grown to nearly 20 venues, with locations in major sports cities across the country. The company expanded its footprint by nearly 50% in 2025 and continues to define itself as a one-of-a-kind destination, pairing strong operations and hospitality with an elevated food and beverage menu in an atmosphere built around the biggest moments for fans. “It’s been a privilege working alongside Shannon, and I’m so proud of what we have built together,” said Brooks Schaden. “Tom’s Watch Bar was incubated at SIF, and is now ready to stand on its own. I’m confident Shannon will continue to successfully guide the team and leverage the incredible momentum we have right now. I look forward to supporting the brand in new ways to help reach the enormous potential we see for Tom’s.” The post Tom’s Watch Bar Names Shannon McNiel CEO appeared first on FSR magazine .

articles.title: Wagamama Rethinks U.S. Growth Strategy
articles.titleKo: Wagamama Rethinks U.S. Growth Strategy
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Wagamama has five U.S. locations. Wagamama has spent more than three decades building a recognizable restaurant brand in the U.K. Its Asian-inspired menu, communal seating, and distinctive dining experience have helped the chain grow to more than 170 locations across its home market. The U.S. has been a different story. Despite operating in America for nearly two decades, Wagamama has just five restaurants, including two in New York City and locations in Boston, Arlington, Virginia, and Tampa, Florida. The brand has struggled to translate its overseas popularity into a meaningful U.S. presence. CEO Stephen Judge believes he knows why. The company initially tried to replicate its successful British restaurant model without sufficiently accounting for differences in American dining habits. “When they brought Wagamama to the U.S., they really brought it with a British playbook, a British recipe book and concept and seating layout that had been proven to be very successful in the U.K. And frankly speaking, they didn’t adapt it for the U.S. market,” Judge says. Judge, a Liverpool native whose restaurant career includes experience with Seasons 52 and Bonefish Grill, was brought aboard to help correct that disconnect and establish a foundation for domestic expansion. One of the first moves involved relocating the company’s U.S. corporate office from Midtown Manhattan to Tampa. His first six months also included extensive consumer research to determine which elements of Wagamama resonated with American guests and which needed to change. The company conducted menu satisfaction studies examining everything from portion sizes and pricing to ingredients and perceived value. Focus groups in New York, Boston, and Washington, D.C., provided additional feedback on restaurant layouts, seating arrangements, and menu presentation. Some of the findings challenged longstanding elements of the Wagamama experience. American guests weren’t particularly fond of the brand’s signature communal tables or backless benches, which they considered uncomfortable during longer dining occasions. They preferred traditional chairs and flexible table configurations that could accommodate different party sizes. Wagamama has since incorporated those preferences into its U.S. restaurants, including locations in Tampa and New York. The research also uncovered some surprising demographic characteristics. Women account for 57 percent of Wagamama’s American customers, and more than 30 percent of its guests earn over $150,000 annually. Those findings helped inform a significant overhaul of the brand’s food and beverage offerings. Wagamama recently introduced 26 new dishes and 15 Asian-inspired drinks, representing one of its most substantial efforts to tailor the concept to American consumers. The additions include Wagamama beef sliders and customizable bao bun tacos, allowing guests to mix different proteins and flavors instead of purchasing two identical buns. New beverage platforms include Wagaritas and Wagatinis, featuring selections such as Thai chili margaritas, lychee martinis, and ube espresso martinis. Judge says the company evaluated more than 250 food items and approximately 150 beverage possibilities before selecting the additions. The objective was to expand the restaurant’s appeal across different dining occasions, from an inexpensive lunch to a multicourse dinner, without abandoning its Asian culinary identity. “Technically, if you wanted to, you could come into Wagamama, get a couple of bao buns and get a juice and be in and out of the restaurant for 20 bucks if you wanted to.” The expanded selection also addresses the veto vote, when one member of a dining party rejects a restaurant because the menu doesn’t offer something appealing. articles.title: The True Cost of a Restaurant Renovation: What Owners Often Overlook
articles.titleKo: The True Cost of a Restaurant Renovation: What Owners Often Overlook
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . The financing structure used for a renovation can influence the restaurant’s financial flexibility long after construction is completed. For full-service restaurant owners, renovations can be an important investment in the future of their business. Updating an aging dining room, replacing kitchen equipment, or redesigning an inefficient layout may improve the guest experience and support long-term growth. However, a restaurant renovation can also create financial challenges that extend well beyond the construction budget. Unexpected expenses, temporary closures, reduced seating capacity, and financing obligations can place significant pressure on cash flow. Before beginning a major renovation, restaurant owners should carefully evaluate the financial decisions that can determine whether the project strengthens the business or creates unnecessary risk. The Construction Estimate Is Not the Entire Budget Restaurant renovation budgets often begin with contractor estimates, equipment costs, and interior improvements. Yet additional expenses can accumulate throughout the project. Permits, architectural services, inspections, technology upgrades, furniture, installation, and unexpected repairs may substantially increase the total investment. Older restaurant properties may also require electrical, plumbing, ventilation, or accessibility improvements that were not anticipated during the initial planning process. Consider a hypothetical full-service restaurant planning a $400,000 renovation. If the owner allocates the entire amount to construction and equipment, an unexpected 15 percent increase in project costs would create an additional $60,000 expense. Without adequate reserves or available financing, the owner may be forced to delay construction, reduce the project’s scope, or use funds intended for normal operations. A realistic renovation budget should include contingency funds and sufficient liquidity to address unexpected expenses. Lost Revenue Can Be More Expensive Than Expected One of the most frequently overlooked renovation costs is the revenue a restaurant may lose while construction is underway. Some projects require a complete temporary closure. Others allow the restaurant to remain open but reduce seating capacity or disrupt normal service. For full-service restaurants, where revenue depends heavily on dining room availability and customer experience, even temporary disruptions can have meaningful financial consequences. Consider a restaurant generating $100,000 in average monthly revenue that expects to operate at 60 percent of its normal sales volume during a two-month renovation. Under that hypothetical scenario, the restaurant would experience approximately $80,000 in revenue reduction compared with its normal sales levels. That figure does not represent an equivalent loss in profit, since certain variable expenses may also decline. However, fixed obligations such as rent, insurance, and some payroll costs may continue. Restaurant owners should estimate how construction will affect both revenue and expenses before committing to a renovation schedule. Whenever possible, owners may benefit from scheduling improvements during historically slower periods or completing construction in phases. Evaluate the Expected Return Not every renovation produces an immediate increase in revenue. Some improvements are necessary to maintain safety, replace aging equipment, or preserve the restaurant’s appearance. Others may be intended to increase seating capacity, improve kitchen efficiency, or attract additional customers. Before investing, owners should distinguish between operational necessities and improvements expected to generate measurable financial returns. The Harvest Stack is sourdough bread piled high with stuffing, garlic red-skin mashed potatoes, grilled turkey breast and a spoonful of cranberry sauce, smothered in turkey gravy. Friendly’s is trading sunshine for snowflakes. Available now through the holiday season, the Snow Days menu brings three seasonal entrées, a peppermint-packed dessert lineup and a pair of value deals to restaurants systemwide. Leading the charge is a trio of stick-to-your-ribs plates made for sweater weather: Snowfall Burger: Friendly’s Big Beef Burger with white American cheese, Alfredo sauce and hardwood-smoked bacon on a Parmesan-dusted pretzel bun, served with golden fries. Fireside Melt: White American cheese and Tillamook sharp yellow cheddar with grilled chicken, hardwood-smoked bacon, tomatoes and garlic aioli on grilled sourdough, paired with golden fries. Harvest Stack: Sourdough bread piled high with stuffing, garlic red-skin mashed potatoes, grilled turkey breast and a spoonful of cranberry sauce, smothered in turkey gravy. To keep spirits bright, guests who order any Snow Days entrée will receive a FREE Happy Ending Sundae, because every good meal deserves a sweet treat. Dessert takes a wintry turn with creations that call for an extra spoon, including: Snowball Fight Sundae: Vanilla ice cream and donut holes dusted with powdered sugar and topped with hot fudge drizzle, mini marshmallows, whipped cream and chocolate sprinkles. Peppermint Stick Fribble: Peppermint Stick ice cream drizzled with hot fudge and crowned with whipped cream and a cherry. Jubilee Cake: A yummy blast from the past, layering chocolate chip and chocolate ice creams beneath fudge drizzle, almonds and chocolate candies, finished with a playful pink frosted border. Value keeps its seat at the table all winter with two deals running alongside the new menu. Better Together pairs two entrées with one appetizer starting at $24.99, or $29.99 for premium entrée picks. For a midday break, the Weekday Lunch Deal offers one of five select entrées plus a Happy Ending Sundae for $11.99, Monday through Friday from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Kids also have another reason to come back, with every kids’ meal including a sealed pack of Conehead Crew trading cards for a chance to complete the 18-card collection. “Friendly’s has always been about making a meal feel like more than just a meal, and Snow Days gives people plenty of ways to have fun,” said Erik Jensen, vice president of marketing for BRIX Holdings. “Between a Snowball Fight Sundae piled high with toppings and a Conehead Crew card pack waiting to be opened, there’s a little something to make every winter visit memorable.” It’s a season of smiles at Friendly’s. Whether stopping in for a quick bite or rounding out a family meal, Friendly’s makes it easy to enjoy the classics without stretching the budget. Guests can also make the most of the new offerings by joining the Friendly’s Fan Club rewards program, which provides exclusive offers, alongside specialty promotions and updates. articles.title: Major Wendy’s Franchisee Significantly Cuts Footprint During Bankruptcy
articles.titleKo: Major Wendy’s Franchisee Significantly Cuts Footprint During Bankruptcy
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . The Wendy's franchisee declared bankruptcy in September. Large Wendy’s franchisee Meritage Hospitality Group has closed 33 Wendy’s restaurants since filing for bankruptcy in September, with another 20–60 shutdowns required by November 13 under a court-approved agreement. The company had already closed approximately 60 underperforming Wendy’s restaurants before bankruptcy, beginning in Q4 2025. Meritage estimated those earlier closures would improve annual EBITDA by $8 million. According to Meritage, these locations were losing money, and shedding their leases and franchise agreements would eliminate unnecessary expenses. The franchisee filed for bankruptcy on September 17 . At filing, it operated 320 restaurants across 15 states, including 314 Wendy’s, and employed approximately 8,850 people. Wendy’s moved to terminate Meritage’s franchise agreements one day before the bankruptcy filing and claims the operator owes roughly $146.9 million in royalties, fees, and other contractual charges. Meritage disputes the termination’s effectiveness and maintains its franchise agreements are still in place. Meritage’s financial troubles intensified over the past two years. Same-store sales fell 7.2 percent in fiscal 2025 and another 8.3 percent during the first half of 2026. The company reported net losses of $31.5 million and $23.1 million during those periods, respectively. The operator attributed its difficulties to weak sales, elevated beef costs, national discounting, disruptive weather, and what it described as less effective Wendy’s marketing under prior brand officials. Before bankruptcy, Meritage pursued cost reductions, changes to breakfast service, and sale-leaseback transactions to improve profitability and reduce debt. Urbane Cafe is growing its Central Coast presence with its new Goleta location, bringing its take on fresh, made-from-scratch dining to the broader Santa Barbara area. Known for its house-baked focaccia, gourmet sandwiches and signature bowls, the California-born brand will welcome guests at its newest location on Monday, October 26. Since opening its doors in Ventura in 2003, Urbane Cafe has set out to make fresh, high-quality food a staple of the fast-casual experience. The brand’s menu features focaccia baked from scratch every day, gourmet sandwiches paired with fresh side salads, hearty bowls and house-made sauces. Each location is an open scratch kitchen with a signature hearth oven, where guests can watch their meals come together. “We love the Central Coast and are excited to bring our scratch-made menu to Goleta,” said Tom Holt, Founder of Urbane Cafe. “The Santa Barbara community has been inquiring about a location for a long time – and we are thrilled that we are able to officially be a part of their amazing community. Their enthusiasm means a lot to us and we look forward to serving them for years to come.” To mark the Goleta debut, Urbane Cafe will celebrate with a lineup of grand opening offerings for community members to enjoy: Grand Opening Day (October 26): The first 50 guests in line will receive a free sandwich every month for a year (12 sandwiches total). A ribbon-cutting ceremony with the Santa Barbara South Coast Chamber of Commerce will take place at 10 a.m. Student Giveback Day (October 28): Students can enjoy a complimentary sandwich, salad or bowl when they order through the Urbane Cafe app with a promotional code. Students must sign up here in advance to receive the code and present a valid student ID at pickup. Limited to 500 Students. Teacher Giveback Day (November 4): Teachers and school staff can enjoy a complimentary sandwich, salad or bowl by completing the RSVP form here to receive a promotional code and placing an online order. This opening comes on the heels of opening the first-ever location in Glendale in September, furthering the brand’s ambitious growth goals. Urbane Cafe plans to open six new Southern California locations in 2027, with a long-term target of 100 total locations by 2030. Building on its active growth into Las Vegas and Arizona, the brand continues to prioritize strategic expansion while preserving the food quality, guest experience and company culture that have defined Urbane Cafe since its founding. Juice It Up!, one of the nation’s leading açai bowl, handcrafted smoothie and raw juice chains for over 30 years, has opened a new location in Temecula, expanding the brand’s presence across Southern California. The new location is owned and operated by Temecula residents Fatemeh Toori and Peyman Zamanian, who plan to grow the brand’s presence throughout the region. Located at Palm Plaza in Temecula, the new Juice It Up! is now proudly serving its signature açaí bowls, blended to order smoothies and fresh-squeezed raw juices to guests seeking delicious options to fuel up on the go. “We were immediately drawn to Juice It Up! for its strong brand foundation, innovative product offerings and reputation for delivering an exceptional guest experience,” said Toori, Juice It Up! Temecula franchisee. “We’re excited to bring that experience to our community and see tremendous opportunity to introduce more Riverside County residents to the brand, build lasting relationships with our guests and grow alongside the community for years to come.” Juice It Up! offers a wide variety of handcrafted menu options that bring flavor and functionality to everyday occasions. An innovator of açaí and lesser-known ingredients since 1995, the brand’s menu includes customizable açaí bowls, blended-to-order smoothies, fresh-squeezed raw juices, toasts, pretzels and more. For more than three decades, Juice It Up! has helped guests “Live Life Juiced!,” a motto that underscores the brand’s longstanding commitment to providing products geared to fuel each day. Juice It Up! This is White Castle’s fifth consecutive year being named to this prestigious list, this year coming in at 11 th place in the large category. Earning a spot means that White Castle is one of the best retail companies to work for in the country. The Best Workplaces in Retail award is based on analysis of survey responses from nearly 76,000 employees at Great Place To Work Certified™ companies in the retail industry. “From our founding in 1921, my great-grandfather Billy Ingram dedicated his leadership to creating a workplace where people are respected, valued and supported,” said John Kelley, chief people officer and fourth-generation family member. “And in the 105 years since, we’ve never wavered on that commitment. It’s an honor to be recognized as a one of the very Best Workplaces in Retail, and we share this recognition with every one of our nearly 9,000 team members.” The Best Workplaces in Retail list is highly competitive. Great Place To Work, the global authority on workplace culture, determines its lists using its proprietary Trust Index™ Survey to evaluate and certify thousands of organizations in America’s largest ongoing annual workforce study, based on over 1.3 million survey responses and data from companies representing more than 7.3 million employees. Survey responses reflect a comprehensive picture of the workplace experience. Honorees were selected based on their ability to offer positive outcomes for employees regardless of job role, work status, or other demographic identifier. “Congratulations to the Fortune Best Workplaces in Retail,” says Michael C. Bush, CEO of Great Place To Work. “People are at the heart of work in every industry, and retail is no exception. These companies show how delivering for your people drives financial performance and turns fear of the future into the confidence to win.” White Castle is widely recognized for its family-centered culture and team member growth. Today, more than one in four team members has been with the business for 10 years or more, and in October White Castle inducted its latest class into the 25-Year Club, which now totals more than 2,500 members. White Castle has been certified as a Great Place to Work every year since 2021 and has been on the Best Workplaces in Retail™ list for five consecutive years — the only restaurant brand to claim this distinction. Pollo Campero, the Guatemalan-born quick-service restaurant known for its fried and roasted chicken, has named industry veteran Julio Sánchez CEO of its U.S. business, effective immediately. The company thanks outgoing chief operating officer Luis Javier Rodas, who concluded nearly 26 years with CMI on Oct. 16, for his contributions to the brand’s growth in the U.S. With more than 25 years of experience, Sánchez has led operations, franchising, development and transformation across North America, Latin America, the Caribbean and Europe. As CEO, Sánchez will lead the next phase of profitable growth for Campero USA, initially focusing on improving operational excellence, accelerating same-store sales growth, increasing brand awareness and elevating the guest experience to bring the Campero flavor to even more consumers across the United States. His appointment comes as the brand grows beyond 150 U.S. restaurants and works toward continued U.S. expansion. Known for his hands-on style, Sánchez leads from the restaurant floor, staying close to the team members, franchise partners and guests who shape the experience every day. “Julio combines deep operational expertise with sound business judgment and a proven record of delivering results. articles.title: Fine-Dining Concept Aria Names Elissa Hayward Executive Pastry Chef
articles.titleKo: Fine-Dining Concept Aria Names Elissa Hayward Executive Pastry Chef
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Aria has named Elissa Hayward executive pastry chef, adding another creative voice to a team where ideas already move between the kitchen, pastry, bar, and wine programs. Hayward reunites with executive chef Austin Goetzman, with whom she previously worked at Lazy Betty, and joins bar lead Eric Simpkins and lead sommelier and assistant general manager Princeton Saunders as the group continues developing, tasting, and exchanging ideas across their respective areas. That collaboration is already taking shape. Hayward and Saunders have been tasting wines for a red wine sorbet, and conversations with Simpkins about smoked flavors have connected what is happening in pastry with what’s happening behind the bar. She and Goetzman regularly taste one another’s work, continuing a creative relationship they first developed while working together previously. “Elissa’s approach immediately stood out to us,” says owner Andrés Loaiza. “She understands the entire kitchen, not just one part of it, and that comes through in the way she thinks about dessert. She has a strong technical foundation, but she also brings curiosity and personality to what she creates. We’re excited to give her the room to explore that at Aria.” For Hayward, joining Aria is an opportunity to develop her own style while working alongside a team whose individual specialties often inform one another. “I think what is exciting is that everyone is really immersed in their own area, but we’re still constantly talking and tasting together,” says Hayward. “Austin is focused on the savory menu, Eric and Princeton are bringing new ideas to the bar and wine programs, and I’m focused on pastry. We all have our own areas, but there is a lot of opportunity for those ideas to come together.” An early glimpse of her approach appears in a dessert Hayward is beginning to develop, featuring smoked vanilla mousse (pictured below), green apple, turmeric, brown butter crumble, and caramel. The combination reflects several elements of her style: familiar flavors and classical technique paired with unexpected ingredients, contrasting textures, and a subtle savory influence. Hayward’s path to pastry has shaped the way she approaches dessert. She trained in both culinary arts and baking and pastry, then spent much of her early career on the savory side of the kitchen before choosing to focus fully on pastry several years ago. Her experience includes time at Bouchon Bistro in California and, most recently, The Deer and the Dove in Decatur. That background still influences her work. Hayward gravitates toward French classics and traditional technique, but she is equally interested in texture, unexpected flavors, and the memories certain ingredients can evoke. A dessert might recall fall, a childhood favorite, or time spent around a campfire, then reinterpret that feeling through a more refined lens. “I love the classics, but I also love playing with nostalgia and finding ways to make something feel familiar and new at the same time,” says Hayward. “There can be something playful about the flavors while there is still a lot of technique behind them. That combination is what I’m always drawn to.” At Aria, Hayward wants pastry to carry the same attention to detail as the savory menu while still giving guests a final course that can surprise them. “I’m excited to involve guests in the pastry side of the menu in the same way they experience the savory side,” says Hayward. “I want dessert to feel like part of the complete meal, with just as much thought behind it, while also giving guests something they may not have expected.” The post Fine-Dining Concept Aria Names Elissa Hayward Executive Pastry Chef appeared first on FSR magazine .

The Cincinnati agreements are the latest example of a broader development surge for Currito, which has now signed 34 franchise units system-wide over the last 22 months and has fully sold-out development rights in the Lexington, Louisville and Dayton markets. A longtime restaurant industry executive, Cunningham spent the last 17 years with One Holland Group, where he joined as controller in 2008 before advancing to chief financial officer and chief development officer. Throughout his career, he has worked across several restaurant brands and gained experience in accounting, finance, development, and day-to-day restaurant operations. His path into restaurants began while attending Ohio State University and later working at Skyline Chili, where he discovered a passion for hospitality, serving others and building strong teams. “After spending nearly two decades in the restaurant industry, I knew I wanted to build something of my own with the right brand and the right people,” said Cunningham. “Currito checked the boxes we were looking for: simple operations, clean and comfortable restaurants, a product people can feel good about and a leadership team that feels like a true partner. Before becoming a franchisee, Patel was first a loyal Currito customer, eating at the restaurant consistently and becoming impressed by the brand’s ability to deliver the same quality, flavor, and experience every time. “Before I ever became a franchisee, I was a Currito customer for two years, and what stood out to me was the consistency,” said Patel . “Every time I came in, the food quality and experience were the same. Michelle Chin spent her first year as Applebee’s CMO visiting restaurants, meeting franchisees, and watching how employees interacted with their regulars. Some guests had favorite seats. Others called ahead to make sure a particular server would be working. A few employees even considered themselves the mayor of the neighborhood. Those relationships gave Chin a starting point for the brand’s marketing. Applebee’s had spent decades building its identity around being a neighborhood gathering place. Inside its restaurants, she found evidence that the promise still meant something. The task now is translating that experience into a reason to visit, including among younger consumers who have chosen other restaurants or have little familiarity with Applebee’s. She sees opportunity in the occasions surrounding the bigger events on people’s calendars. A family can stop in before a game. Friends can catch up after a movie. Sunday church services can lead to a meal together. None requires a birthday, holiday, or elaborate plan.` “It’s all about that human connection and that socialization at the table where people can have a conversation,” Chin says. “And it could be big conversations, but even more importantly, it’s those little moments. Sure, I would love game days and birthdays and all of that. But I think what’s even more important are those in-between moments. And I’ve been playing with this notion of, really wanting people to get together at Applebee’s on those pre and post moments around the main event and their lives.” That thinking gives Applebee’s a role in everyday life that Chin wants its marketing to communicate more clearly. The restaurant can be an easy place to reconnect, with familiar food and a setting that doesn’t demand much preparation. “I think we’ve put this whole notion of dining out on a pedestal and it makes it hard and kind of like out of touch with it. And so make it casual again. Like I just want to connect. I just want to see you. Let’s just grab some wings,” Chin says. Making that message relevant involves changes across marketing and the menu. During her first year, Chin has added talent, tested products, and increased the brand’s participation in social conversations. Applebee’s also named BBDO Chicago its new creative agency of record, following nearly a decade with Grey. The roster includes new vice presidents of integrated marketing and culinary. Chin sees those positions as important to connecting the brand’s message with what guests actually encounter when they sit down to eat. A social team that came aboard shortly before her arrival has helped Applebee’s listen to customers and identify conversations where it can participate naturally. Chin says the brand has seen traffic gains among Gen Z consumers. The objective is to earn a place in people’s daily conversations without turning every interaction into a product pitch. “When we do jump into the conversation and be part of their everyday conversation, the brand’s showing up authentically,” Chin says. “We’re not trying to hard sell anything.
