articles.title: Whataburger Bringing the Heat with Holiday Menu
articles.titleKo: Whataburger Bringing the Heat with Holiday Menu
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . This holiday season, Whataburger is bringing the heat, the holiday cheer and plenty of bold flavors to the table. Beginning Oct. 20, the Bacon Blaze lineup fires up the menu with the fan-favorite Bacon Blaze Jalapeño Double and new Bacon Blaze Chicken, both packing the perfect kick. And for Guests who’d rather sip than sizzle, the Sleigh Berry Whatafresher and the Whataburger White Chocolate Raspberry Shake give Guests two festive ways to satisfy their sweet tooth. The full limited-time lineup includes: Bacon Blaze Jalapeño Double – The Bacon Blaze lineup offers just the right amount of heat that never sacrifices flavor. The Bacon Blaze Jalapeño Double layers two fresh, 100% beef patties with creamy Jalapeño Ranch, jalapeño cream cheese, smoky bacon, sliced jalapeños and real aged cheddar cheese. Guests looking for a smaller bite can order it in a Jr. size. Bacon Blaze Chicken – The new Bacon Blaze Chicken puts that same perfect kick on premium chicken, with Guests’ choice of grilled or Whatachick’n® on a toasted potato bun. Sleigh Berry Whatafresher – The new Sleigh Berry Whatafresher is a bright, festive refresher that brings together tart cranberry, juicy citrus and a hint of cozy holiday warmth for a perfectly balanced seasonal sip. Real cranberry pieces and a lightly sweet, creamy soft whip make it even more festive. White Chocolate Raspberry Shake – For dessert, the new Whataburger White Chocolate Raspberry Shake pairs sweet white chocolate and tart raspberry flavors in a creamy vanilla shake that tastes like white chocolate raspberry cheesecake. “Guests are looking for more variety from restaurant menus — from bold, spicy flavors to beverages that feel fresh and seasonal,” said Whataburger Corporate Chef James Sanchez. “This lineup lets us deliver both: bringing back a flavor Guests have already told us they love while introducing new choices that feel right for the season.” The Bacon Blaze Jalapeño Double starts at $9.99, with the Jr. Bacon Blaze Jalapeño Double and Bacon Blaze Chicken starting at $7.99. The Sleigh Berry Whatafresher starts at $3.69, and the White Chocolate Raspberry Shake starts at $3.99. Prices vary by location. The whole lineup is only around for a limited time at participating locations, so get it while you can. Hungry for more? Whataburger serves fans 24/7, whether they swing through the drive-thru, order online or use the Whataburger App. Guests who download the app and create an account automatically receive a free Whataburger and begin earning points toward their favorite menu items. Visit Whataburger.com for more details. The post Whataburger Bringing the Heat with Holiday Menu appeared first on QSR Magazine .

articles.title: Newport Beach’s Sushi Ii Changes Name to Sushi Suhama
articles.titleKo: Newport Beach’s Sushi Ii Changes Name to Sushi Suhama
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Sushi Ii, the intimate Japanese restaurant in Newport Beach’s Mariner’s Mile, has entered its next chapter as Sushi Suhama, with a new name that reflects both the restaurant’s Japanese roots and its connection to the coastal landscape it calls home. While the name is new, Sushi Suhama remains an evolution of the restaurant guests have come to know, continuing its commitment to seasonality, craftsmanship, and traditional Japanese culinary technique. The intimate setting and culinary team that have defined the restaurant remain at the heart of Sushi Suhama. Since opening, the restaurant has been recognized by the MICHELIN Guide six times, a distinction Sushi Suhama carries with it into this next chapter. The name Suhama comes from an ancient Japanese term referring to a beautiful or picturesque shoreline. For the restaurant, Suhama evokes the natural shoreline that defines Newport Beach, creating a connection between Japanese culture and the coastal setting that has been part of the restaurant’s identity since opening. Renowned Japanese artist Hiroshi Sugimoto was commissioned to help shape this next chapter and selected the name Sushi Suhama for the restaurant. One of Sugimoto’s celebrated seascapes will also be displayed within the space, further connecting the restaurant’s new identity to the meeting of sea, landscape, and Japanese artistry. “Suhama felt meaningful because it gives the restaurant a sense of place. This is still the restaurant our guests know, but the new name gives us an opportunity to express more clearly who we are today and where we are going, while remaining true to what has always defined the experience,” said Director Natsuko Travioli. Along with the new identity, Sushi Suhama has refined its omakase offerings to give guests distinct ways to experience the restaurant. The Sai Kaiseki Course offers the most expansive progression through the traditions of Japanese multi-course dining, while the new Ran Signature Course balances composed seasonal dishes with a greater emphasis on sushi. The Mio Sushi Course places nigiri at the center of the experience, offering the most sushi-forward expression of the three. The new structure allows guests to choose the style of omakase experience that most appeals to them, from a complete kaiseki progression to an experience centered more heavily around sushi. Across each, menus continue to evolve with the seasons and the availability of ingredients at their peak. The evolution comes under the continued culinary leadership of Chefs Norio Izawa and Koji Takahashi, alongside Director Natsuko Travioli. Izawa heads Sushi Suhama’s kaiseki program, drawing upon his training in respected kaiseki kitchens in Tokyo and Kanazawa and experience at Nobu in New York and Bluefin in Newport Beach to guide the restaurant’s multi-course culinary experience. Takahashi, who has been with the restaurant since its opening and brings nearly four decades of experience to his craft, leads the sushi program. Working alongside him is Chef Tatsushi Wakabayashi, who joined the team approximately a year ago and brings experience from Nobu, Ikko, and Oshima. Together, the chefs preserve the discipline and precision of traditional Japanese cooking while allowing the experience to evolve with a modern sensibility. That philosophy extends beyond the menu. From the ceramics selected for each presentation to the intimate counter experience and considered pace of service, Sushi Suhama remains rooted in the Japanese belief that hospitality is expressed through attention to detail. The restaurant’s new identity builds upon that foundation rather than redefining it, marking a natural evolution of a restaurant that has continued to refine itself since opening. articles.titleKo: Corner Bakery Cafe Adds New Franchisee in Pennsylvania
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . TJ Rice brings more than five years of restaurant and hospitality experience. Corner Bakery Cafe is welcoming a new franchise partner in Pennsylvania as TJ Rice, founder of Rice Equity Group, takes ownership of its Horsham cafe. Rice adds Corner Bakery to a multi-brand portfolio that includes Subway, Captain D’s and Massage Envy, bringing an experienced operator with existing business and family ties to the Philadelphia region into the brand’s growing franchise network. “Welcoming experienced operators like TJ is an important part of how we’re building Corner Bakery’s future,” said Erin Hasselgren, president of Corner Bakery Cafe. “He brings a strong operating foundation, a focus on developing teams and a personal appreciation for the guest experience that defines our cafes. We’re excited to welcome him to the Corner Bakery family and support his investment in the PA Market.” Rice brings more than five years of restaurant and hospitality experience, with a focus on multi-unit operations, franchise development and team leadership. Through Rice Equity Group, he emphasizes consistent guest experiences, strong operating systems and opportunities for employees to develop and advance. For Rice, joining Corner Bakery also builds on a connection formed as a guest. He and his family have enjoyed visiting the brand’s cafes throughout the Washington, D.C., Maryland and Virginia region, drawn to the inviting atmosphere and variety of food. “We have tremendous confidence in Erin Hasselgren’s leadership and his vision for the future of Corner Bakery Cafe,” said Rice. “At Rice Equity Group, we are deliberate in selecting the brands and leadership teams with whom we partner, and we see an exceptional opportunity to grow alongside Erin and the Corner Bakery team. Our ambition is to become one of Corner Bakery’s most trusted and valued franchise partners, bringing the operational infrastructure, financial discipline, experienced leadership, and multi-unit execution capabilities necessary to support disciplined expansion.” Rice’s family and business interests already have roots in Pennsylvania. His wife is a Temple University alumna, and the couple owns and operates health and wellness clinics in the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh markets. Taking ownership of the Horsham cafe builds on those connections and his commitment to continued investment in the region. The Horsham acquisition marks the beginning of Rice Equity Group’s investment in Corner Bakery, with Rice looking to build a broader presence with the brand. His long-term commitment reflects the opportunity he sees in Corner Bakery’s future and adds an experienced, growth-minded partner to its franchise network. For more information, visit cornerbakerycafe.com or follow Corner Bakery Cafe on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, or TikTok. articles.title: Vicious Biscuit Signs Deal to Open in Valdosta, Georgia
articles.titleKo: Vicious Biscuit Signs Deal to Open in Valdosta, Georgia
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Vicious Biscuit, the original home of unapologetically bold biscuits, has signed veteran restaurant operators Doug Puryear and Brian Smith as franchise partners in South Georgia. The longtime business partners, who own and operate nine Surcheros restaurants, will open their first Vicious Biscuit in Valdosta, with an anticipated spring 2027 opening. The agreement marks Vicious Biscuit’s entry into the market as the Charleston-born fast-casual breakfast and brunch brand continues expanding across the Southeast and Midwest. Puryear and Smith, whose restaurant group operates as SAP Saint Simons, bring 30 years of combined restaurant industry experience to Vicious Biscuit. Puryear has spent 10 years in the business, while Smith has 20 years, including a decade owning two Hardee’s locations. Together, they previously operated two Huddle House restaurants for 10 years. Their Surcheros locations in Valdosta and Brunswick consistently rank among the brand’s top performers. Their interest in Vicious Biscuit began when Puryear visited the brand’s flagship restaurant in Mount Pleasant, SC. Impressed by the food and guest experience, he encouraged Smith to visit. After experiencing the concept firsthand and meeting with Vicious Biscuit’s leadership team, the partners decided to add the brand to their restaurant portfolio. “The food is what initially got our attention, but the more we learned about Vicious Biscuit, the more impressed we became,” said Puryear. “We’ve worked with several restaurant brands over the years, and the operations, technology and support systems Vicious Biscuit has already put in place really stood out. They’ve built a strong foundation, and we wanted to be part of it.” The partners were also attracted to Vicious Biscuit’s single-daypart operating model, which focuses on breakfast and brunch. Having previously operated 24-hour restaurants, they recognized the appeal of a more focused approach to staffing, restaurant operations and the guest experience. “Vicious Biscuit has put a lot of thought into how the business operates,” said Smith. “The leadership team understands what franchisees need, and they’ve built the systems to support them. At the same time, the food and hospitality are what make the brand different. That’s an important combination for us.” The approximately 4,000-square-foot Valdosta restaurant will be located at 3259 Inner Perimeter Road, Suite G, in the North Oak Square Shopping Center, adjacent to the partners’ existing Surcheros restaurant. The restaurant is expected to seat 80 to 90 guests. “Doug and Brian have a proven track record of operating successful restaurants and building strong teams,” said George McLaughlin, co-founder and CEO of Vicious Biscuit. “They’re actively involved in their businesses, understand their markets and share our commitment to great food and hospitality. They’re exactly the kind of experienced operators we want to grow with.” As Vicious Biscuit expands into new markets, the brand continues to invest in franchise training, operational systems and technology to support its single-daypart restaurant model. Vicious Biscuit currently operates 13 restaurants, including seven corporate and six franchise locations, with eight additional franchise units signed and under development. Another 33 restaurants are committed under existing franchise agreements, with development contingent upon securing leases. Vicious Biscuit is seeking multiunit operators to join its growing franchise system. For more information, visit www.viciousbiscuit.com/vicious-biscuit-franchise . Visit www.viciousbiscuit.com for additional brand updates. Follow on Instagram @viciousbiscuits, Facebook at ViciousBiscuit1, and TikTok @viciousbiscuitchs to stay in the loop as we continue making big moves and bold biscuit creations. Sweetgreen today announced it is rolling out a refreshed Housemade Beverage lineup, including two new flavors. Tropical Black Tea and Fresh Blackberry Basil will join updated recipes for two customer favorites, the Signature Lemonade and Ginger Greens, across 120 locations. The refresh will also include a new 24oz cup size in addition to the existing 16oz offering. Drinks are made fresh in-house from real fruit, vegetables, fresh herbs and agave as a sweetener. The new Tropical Black Tea contains no sweetener. The drinks are a natural extension of how sweetgreen has always approached food: start with real, whole ingredients and let them lead. Guests are making drinks part of their sweetgreen routine, whether it’s paired with lunch or as an afternoon pick-me-up. The share of transactions including a beverage has increased nearly 25% since sweetgreen introduced its initial housemade beverages at participating locations. The refresh builds on that momentum, with each drink designed to elevate the overall dining experience, creating pairings that feel intentional and balanced. “At sweetgreen, we’re always exploring new ways to bring bold, delicious flavors to the menu,” said Nicolas Jammet, Co-Founder and Chief Concept Officer of sweetgreen. “We made them slightly less sweet so the blackberry, basil and ginger come through first, and every drink is crafted to complement the meal. A drink is often the last thing someone adds to their order, and we want it to be one of the parts they look forward to most.” The Housemade Beverage lineup includes: Tropical Black Tea (NEW) – Bold black tea with tropical fruit and toasted coconut notes. Fresh Blackberry Basil (NEW) – Juicy blackberry with fresh, fragrant basil. Signature Lemonade (REFRESHED) – Bright, citrusy, and exceptionally refreshing. Ginger Greens (REFRESHED) – Sweet apple, fresh spinach, and zesty ginger. Order in-store, on the sweetgreen app or at sweetgreen.com for pickup or delivery, and follow @sweetgreen on Instagram and TikTok for the latest. articles.title: McDonald’s and ‘Top Chef’ Winner Tristen Epps-Long Unveil One-Day Chef’s Table Experience

articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . McDonald's is inviting fans to experience a curated tasting menu of its iconic menu items at Inside the Golden Arches, the brand's first-ever chef’s table experience, taking place in New York City on October 29. Ever wondered what makes a Quarter Pounder with Cheese sandwich so craveable? Why the egg on an Egg McMuffin breakfast sandwich is perfectly round? Or what goes into the fries you’ve loved for years? On October 29, fans in New York City can snag a seat and find out for themselves. For one day only, McDonald’s and “Top Chef” Season 22 winner and former McDonald’s Crew member Tristen Epps-Long are opening the doors to Inside the Golden Arches , a complimentary chef’s table experience where fans can hear directly from chefs and experts about the quality ingredients, attention to detail and small touches behind some of McDonald’s most iconic menu items. Stepping into the spotlight is the hot and deliciously juicy Quarter Pounder with Cheese. Guests will see how it’s prepared, from the 100% real beef cooked fresh when ordered to the simple ingredients that make it a fan favorite. They’ll also enjoy other McDonald’s iconic menu items, including the Egg McMuffin, Chicken McNuggets and World Famous Fries. Is your mouth watering yet? Chef Tristen will guide guests through the experience, sharing his perspective as a chef—and as one of the 1 in 8 Americans who have worked behind the counter at McDonald’s. “McDonald’s was where I got my start, and the experience helped shape the way I think about food and hospitality,” said Chef Tristen. “Even now, I have a deep appreciation for the consistency that allows millions of people to enjoy the same great meal wherever they are. Inside the Golden Arches gives fans a rare opportunity to see the people, processes and care behind that experience.” While seats at the table are limited, the Quarter Pounder with Cheese celebration is just getting started. Beginning Nov. 2, fans across the country can enjoy the Quarter Pounder with Cheese complete with medium fries and a drink for just $8, at participating McDonald’s restaurants. “Inside the Golden Arches is about creating a new level of access and transparency for our fans,” said Gina Hardy, Vice President, U.S. Marketing & Menu Strategy. “People know the Quarter Pounder with Cheese as one of McDonald’s most iconic burgers, but they may not know that it’s made with 100% beef, never frozen, delivered to local restaurants 2-3 times a week and grilled once you order. We’re excited to give fans a firsthand look at these quality ingredients and gold standard practices, helping them see what makes McDonald’s uniquely McDonald’s.” READY TO PULL UP A CHAIR? articles.title: Pancheros Plays the Long Game on Value and Growth
articles.titleKo: Pancheros Plays the Long Game on Value and Growth
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Pancheros has around 75 restaurants systemwide. Back to normal. It’s a state of being restaurants have been scratching and clawing for in the years since the pandemic sent shockwaves through the industry. For Pancheros founder and CEO Rodney Anderson, 2026 has proven to be the year that the phrase has actually become real. “We’ve been working really hard and trying to make the unit level economics exactly what they were before the pandemic, and I think we’ve done a great job with that,” Anderson says. The roughly 75-unit Pancheros worked with suppliers to mitigate protein costs and leveraged AI tools to better calculate the right yield amounts and reduce waste. As a result, according to Anderson, Pancheros is back to the lowest food cost it’s ever had, even with continued cost increases related to taxes, digital services, and other expenses. Franchisees appear to be on board with the brand’s direction, especially because of better operations. Pancheros has focused on remodeling older locations with digital make lines, a feature that’s led to increases in overall sales—not just digital. That’s in addition to better customer satisfaction, more efficient throughput, and lower employee turnover. More digital make lines are being added to restaurants each week. “First you say, ‘Well, digital sales should go up, but you don’t realize that the in-restaurant guest really likes being treated properly, and those digital sales and the old design with the single make line were interfering with the in-restaurant experience. So that pain went away,” Anderson says. “…It is great for business. It really helps with those peak periods. And not just in handling the third party and the digital stuff, but handling the overall restaurant and the entire package—the entire experience that the customer has.” The rise in digital sales, which account for about 33 percent of sales, has coincided with increased loyalty membership. This year, Pancheros reached 1 million members, or about 13,500 per location. About 26.17 percent of members actively participate. These guests have access to promotions around National Burrito Day, Cinco de Mayo, Teacher Appreciation, and more. Pancheros plans to offer a Halloween BOGO deal for its loyalty members next week. “During the pandemic, we had a real strategy to push digital. Only a couple weeks into it, we realized that we had to have that pickup and delivery work, and we took our entire budget and canceled a lot of projects, canceled a lot of creative, and we really pushed it into developing digital, and our digital grew like crazy, and it’s really given us an advantage over other restaurant chains,” Anderson says. Anderson describes these promotions as rewarding loyal customers as opposed to discounting. The executive says Pancheros is in an advantageous position because it limited price increases a few years after the pandemic. The chain raised prices no more than 4 percent, he says. So for those brands that may have implemented double-digit price increases, guests are pushing back, according to Anderson. The same isn’t happening for Pancheros because of its willingness to accept lower margins in the short term. “We have kept our prices low. We will probably see a price increase this spring again, probably no more than a few percent. And we just want to treat the customers right, and be concerned with long-run sales and value with them, and not go out and start doing these bundled meals and discounts and things like that,” Anderson says. “But we do have a good loyalty program where we do reward them for eating there, and we do some promotions to bring them in. articles.title: 99 Sushi Bar & Restaurant to Debut in Mayfair This November, Marking the Brand’s First UK Opening

Located at 22 Park Lane, the opening marks a significant milestone for 99 Sushi Bar & Restaurant as it enters the UK market for the first time, joining an established international portfolio spanning Madrid, Barcelona, Marbella, Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Monaco, Rabat and Budapest. Since its beginnings in Madrid, 99 Sushi Bar & Restaurant has developed an international trajectory underpinned by prestigious gastronomic recognition across multiple markets. Its Abu Dhabi restaurant has held a MICHELIN Star for three consecutive years, while both Abu Dhabi and Dubai were awarded One Toque by Gault&Millau in 2024. A Contemporary Expression of Japanese Culinary Art 99 Sushi Bar & Restaurant Mayfair presents an elegant and modern interpretation of traditional Japanese cuisine, elevated through precise craftsmanship and an uncompromising approach to ingredient sourcing. At the core of its offering is a commitment to premium produce, notably Atlantic fatty bluefin tuna, and a culinary philosophy rooted in near-perfect execution “99% perfect,” reflecting the brand’s belief that absolute perfection remains unattainable. The menu is designed as a journey through refined Japanese gastronomy, subtly infused with European techniques and influences inspired by the travels of founders Pedro and Fernando de León. This fusion creates a distinctive culinary identity that challenges conventional expectations of a traditional sushi restaurant. Interiors feature gold accents, mirrored surfaces, amber-lit textures and rich velvet tones in purple and crimson, creating an intimate and atmospheric dining environment. Designed to evolve from day into evening, the design combines luminous winter whites with deeper, warming tones, to create a sense of discovery throughout the property. At the heart of the experience, the Lobby will bloom into a grand Winter Garden, guiding guests to Palm Court for the hotel’s celebrated afternoon tea. In Palm Court, guests can take in ‘The Blooming Winter Garden’, inspired by the Victorian glasshouses that allowed exotic plants and fruits to flourish throughout winter. The Winter Garden Festive Afternoon Tea (available 9 November 2026 to 3 January 2027) will feature seasonal flavours, with finger sandwiches such as Roast Bronze Turkey, stu1ing, pickled cranberries and chestnut with a delicate savoury of Potato farl, crème fraiche and oscietra caviar. Snowy white throughout, with bright pops of colour, the cakes and pastries will showcase the likes of Plum and Ginger and Chestnut and Blackcurrant, all in which will be served alongside scones with clotted cream, preserves, a showstopping sharing cake, alongside The Langham’s Glasshouse; an Earl Grey infused layered sponge with bergamot jelly. As day turns to night, ‘Midnight in the Winter Garden’ will see Artesian cocktail bar transformed into a shimmering evening setting inspired by the season. Head Bartender Giulia Cuccurullo and the talented team at Artesian have created two exclusive festive cocktails for the occasion, the Pineapple & Brioche, a decadent take on the Ramos Gin Fizz, combining caramelised rum with bright pineapple and citrus, balanced by rich brioche notes and finished with a velvety foam and the Fig & Port, a luxurious cocktail inspired by the Manhattan, pairing crisp vodka with rich fig and warming aged port, lifted by the dry, saline character of fino sherry. Hearty dishes made with seasonal ingredients will be served alongside the festive drinks we all crave as the temperature drops. The celebrations continue across The Langham, London on New Year’s Eve, with a choice of three ways to see out 2026 in style. In Palm Court, guests can enjoy an elegant five-course dinner, beginning with Champagne and canapés and accompanied by live music throughout the evening. articles.title: The £95 Restaurant Ripple Effect: How Dining Out Drives Spending Beyond the Bill
articles.titleKo: The £95 Restaurant Ripple Effect: How Dining Out Drives Spending Beyond the Bill
articles.originalSummary: For more than 25 years, OpenTable has worked alongside restaurants to help them fill tables, connect with diners and grow their businesses. Its 2026 Restaurant Impact Report explores the vital role restaurants play in local economies, communities and everyday life, as well as how diners can help them thrive. The findings demonstrate that restaurants contribute far more than dining alone. They drive spending and footfall for surrounding businesses while creating spaces where people can come together and reconnect. The report explores the challenges restaurants face, including the impact of no-shows, and how small actions from diners can make a meaningful difference. Among the findings: Dining out has an economic ripple effect: 56% of UK diners spend at neighbouring businesses before or after their meal, spending an average of £95. Restaurants bring people together: 98% say local restaurants are important to their community, while 71% of Gen Z diners are likely to book a meal out to feel better or reconnect when they feel stressed or low. Supporting restaurants goes beyond the bill: Among Gen Z diners who made a restaurant reservation in the past year, 57% admit to having failed to show up at least once. A no-show for a table of two costs £55.70 on average, according to restaurant workers,² while 48% say understanding the financial impact of a no-show would make them more likely to honour or cancel a booking. “Restaurants are so much more than places to eat, they create jobs, bring people together and play an important role in the life of communities across the UK,” explains Sasha Shaker, Senior Director of Restaurant Sales and Service, OpenTable UK and Ireland . “This report showcases the industry’s wider impact and highlights why restaurants matter and why OpenTable is dedicated to advocating for their success.” Restaurants Fuel Employment and Local Economies More than half (56%) of UK restaurant diners said they spent money on other activities the last time they ate out locally.¹ Those who spent elsewhere alongside their meal spent £95.20 on average, rising to £126 among Gen Z and £118 among Millennials.¹ Restaurants see this impact first-hand, with 51% of hospitality workers saying their restaurant drives footfall or spending at nearby businesses. According to UKHospitality, hospitality is the UK’s third-largest employer, with restaurants employing 1.3 million people and contributing £44 billion to the economy annually. Restaurants Drive Community and Personal Wellbeing Restaurants provide spaces where people meet, celebrate and connect. More than half (56%) of UK diners are likely to book a meal out to feel better when stressed or low, rising to 71% among Gen Z diners.¹ If their favourite local restaurant disappeared tomorrow, 53% would miss the atmosphere and character it brings. Dr Martha Newson, Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Greenwich , explains: “Sharing a meal at a restaurant is one of the oldest ways of bringing people together, because sitting around a table lets us focus on each other. Our research with over 10,000 people worldwide found face-to-face contact remains a strong predictor of wellbeing, as social bonds deepen through eye contact and shared experiences.” The Balancing Act for Restaurants While restaurants support their local areas, they are also navigating significant pressures. OpenTable’s research found that if VAT were reduced from 20% and restaurants passed the savings on through lower menu prices, 39% of diners would eat out more often, while a further 22% would spend more when they did. The report also explores how restaurants could use potential VAT savings. According to the research, 42% would primarily use a reduction to protect or increase staff wages and hours, 31% would lower menu prices for customers and 30% would reduce how often they need to raise prices. Serve First , the operational excellence platform for customer experience across multi-location service businesses, today announced the expansion of its US operations. Brad Christian joins as Managing Director and will lead Serve First in the US from its office in Alpharetta, GA. Brad brings more than 20 years of experience working with clients in the customer experience industry. He was previously Chief Customer Officer at a customer experience consultancy and Chief Commercial Officer for the experience practice of a global market research firm. He has helped brands design and deploy measurement systems that drive strategic insight and deliver real business performance improvement. The US office supports the global expansion of existing client programs. Serve First is building US customer success and marketing teams to serve those and other US-based clients. Brad will work with brands across restaurants, hotels and hospitality, convenience stores and retail petroleum, and facilities management. Most US operators already measure plenty, through surveys, audits, mystery shops and review tracking. The problem is that many times nothing changes at the location because of it. The report arrives next month, and the site manager never sees it. Serve First captures every signal in one platform, from guest feedback and audits to mystery shopping. EVA, the analyst built into the platform, measures each location against the brand’s own standards, finds where it falls short and why, and builds the plan to fix it. The fix goes to the person who can make it, with proof it got done. “Traditional CX programs have many times been more of an academic exercise than a true focus on actually impacting the customer experience,” said Brad Christian, Managing Director, Serve First. “These programs have been optimized for collecting data, but they lack the actionability to drive meaningful change at the front line. Metrics matter, but meaning matters more. When teams have the feedback, the right tasks and the support to change how they work, brands deliver better customer experiences.” “Brad knows what it takes to turn customer experience programs into real change at every location,” said Erol Ayvaz, CEO, Serve First. “Expanding our US operations under his leadership is the next step in Serve First’s global growth, and it gives our US clients a team on the ground.” The post Brad Christian Joins Serve First as Managing Partner to Lead U.S. Expansion appeared first on QSR Magazine .

articles.title: 5 Lessons in Leadership from WiRL Keynote Speaker Meg Farren
articles.titleKo: 5 Lessons in Leadership from WiRL Keynote Speaker Meg Farren
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Meg Farren’s path to president of Taco Bell North America ran through JPMorgan, strategy consulting, luxury desserts, grocery retail, and a decade at KFC, where she led a brand turnaround. Then came her biggest move yet: a transatlantic relocation with her family to lead one of the most beloved brands in the world. In a conversation with QSR magazine earlier this year , she reflected on what she has learned along the way. Listen before you lead When Farren started at Taco Bell, she skipped the big pronouncements and went on a listening tour, traveling with second- and third-generation franchisees and learning from managers. “Sometimes you see people come into a new role and feel like they have to prove themselves by telling others what they should be doing,” Farren says. “But the heart of great trust and collaboration is an ability to listen really well and slowly start to say, ‘Have we tried this?’” Registration is now open for Year 4 of the Women in Restaurant Leadership Summit! Bring your whole self to work Farren doesn’t pretend the juggle isn’t real, and she doesn’t expect her team to either. Instead, she tries to create space for openness and vulnerability, starting with her own. “I am a whole person, not just a work person, and most people are juggling the same kinds of trade-offs and priorities at home that I am,” Farren says. “I try to be a role model to my team that yes, we’re all trying to make our lives work.” Stay healthily dissatisfied Taco Bell can turn a great idea around in two weeks, which is rare for a company of its size. Farren credits a culture that never settles and isn’t afraid to disrupt the status quo through thoughtful innovation. “Taco Bell operates like an $18 billion startup, and to execute brilliantly at our size requires a certain culture and level of partnership across the entire business,” Farren says. “There is this constant healthy dissatisfaction with the status quo, and every franchisee can tell you that we are relentlessly innovating for the next generation of growth.” Never underestimate a thank-you To Farren, culture isn’t a corporate slogan. It’s a set of daily behaviors, shaped at every level of the organization in ways seen and unseen, and recognition is one of the most powerful. “You don’t always show up in your best form every day,” Farren says, “but I do try to make sure all voices are heard in the room, that I foster a culture of recognition, and I’m saying ‘thank you’ and recognizing the contributions of others.” Take the big leap, even when life is messy Farren spent six months commuting from London while her kids finished the school year, building relationships over Zoom while managing what she calls “life admin” and big emotions. “I was getting to know a new organization and learning how to navigate these relationships while driving great performance and delivering well for your team and customers—all while managing a huge family transition,” Farren reflects. “I have depths of resilience, and I’ve been lucky to land with a team who cares about me … it’s been a big step up, but totally worth it.” Hear more from Farren live in Scottsdale. She will deliver the afternoon keynote at WiRL 2027, Feb. 7-9, 2027, at the Grand Hyatt Scottsdale Resort, alongside fellow keynoters Nivera Wallani and Amy Ellis Durini of KFC. WiRL has sold out three years running, and registrations are outpacing every previous year. Save your seat here. articles.title: Cheba Hut to Open in South Scottsdale, Arizona
articles.titleKo: Cheba Hut to Open in South Scottsdale, Arizona
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . A fresh place to grab a bite, kick back with a cold drink and stay awhile is headed to South Scottsdale. Cheba Hut “Toasted” Subs , the counter-culture sandwich shop known for its chill atmosphere, cottonmouth cures, and bold flavors that hit just right, arrives Oct. 26, planted at 2200 N. Scottsdale Road, Suite 110, south of Oak Street and north of McDowell Road. Just south of Old Town Scottsdale, with its world-class shopping, buzzing nightlife, major events and tightly packed arts scene, the restaurant sits close to some of the region’s go-to outings. Guests can fuel up before visiting the Phoenix Zoo, swing by after exploring Papago Park, stop in on the way to Scottsdale Stadium during Cactus League season or make a side quest out of browsing The Antique Trove, Scottsdale Pawn Shop and Sidewalk Surfer Skate Shop. South Scottsdale marks the 13 th Cheba Hut in the Phoenix area and the latest milestone in a fast run for franchise owners Justin and Michelle Lemos, who now operate five shops in less than two years. They launched in North Scottsdale in February 2025, followed with the 101 and Shea a month later, additionally taking over Paradise Valley from Cheba Hut headquarters in January and adding Arcadia in June. “Long before we owned a Cheba Hut, we were regulars who came in for the best sandwich we’d ever had and stuck around for the music, the art and a crew that actually loved being there,” said Justin Lemos, franchise owner. “Those folks are still what it’s all about for us. We promote from within and hire locally, so every opening creates a path for someone on our team to step into something bigger. South Scottsdale means more homegrown careers taking root right alongside the subs.” Like every destination across the Chebaverse, the location tells a local story on its walls. Joshua Finley, who has left his mark on more than 50 Cheba Hut locations nationwide, reimagining the surrounding Old Town “village” as a scene straight out of an anime series. Additional Cheba Hut references fill the frame, along with Easter eggs that reward a second look (and maybe a third). Beyond the centerpiece mural, the space doubles as a showcase for Valley creators, featuring work by pop cannabis artist Aubri Swell ( @MaryJaneArtCompany ) and wood artist Basile Taylor ( @BasileMakesThings ). The owners plan to extend that spotlight to more makers and artisans, with original art for sale so fans can take a little piece of Cheba home. Behind the counter, a full-service bar pours liquor, beer and wine from shelves meant to keep changing. The team will keep adding bottles and taps based on Arizona favorites and crowd requests, so the lineup grows right alongside the neighborhood. For first-timers, Cheba Hut serves more than 30 signature toasted subs named for classic strains and available in Nug (4-inch), Pinner (8-inch) and Blunt (12-inch) sizes. Regulars reach for the White Widow, stacked with chicken, bacon and ranch. The Kali Mist turns up the heat on a club piled with turkey, pepper jack and more of that bacon. The Dank layers pepperoni, salami, marinara and melted mozzarella into a pizza-inspired build, and the Griefo goes green with cream cheese, avocado and fresh vegetables. For something beyond the main event, the menu has plenty of options built for late-night cravings, from pretzel nugs and garlic cheese bread to Krispy Bars, goo balls and cookies, plus the Kool-Aid that’s been quenching thirst since day one. Cheba Hut South Scottsdale will be open Sunday through Thursday from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m., with extended hours until midnight Friday and Saturday. With its mix of toasted sandwiches, unserious humor, neighborhood-first mindset and a disrespectful mascot named “Flip the Bird,” Cheba Hut is ready to make Scottsdale a little more dank, one sub at a time. articles.title: Maine’s White Barn Inn Welcomes Executive Chef Cornelia Sühr
articles.titleKo: Maine’s White Barn Inn Welcomes Executive Chef Cornelia Sühr
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . From a working barn to celebrated culinary destination, White Barn Inn, Auberge Collection has spent more than five decades evolving alongside the landscape that surrounds it. Once home to livestock, horses and chickens – and later used as an ice creamery – the historic barn was restored in 1973 and transformed into White Barn Inn Restaurant, establishing a legacy of elevated dining rooted in Maine’s agricultural and coastal bounty. This autumn, the acclaimed restaurant enters a new culinary chapter under Executive Chef Cornelia Sühr, whose international fine-dining career brings a distinctly European perspective to the New England landmark. German-born, Sühr has worked in some of the world’s most acclaimed kitchens, including Alain Ducasse at The Dorchester and The Savoy in London, and later at The Carlyle, A Rosewood Hotel in New York, where she became the hotel’s first female Chef de Cuisine. She went on to lead kitchens at Jean-Georges Philadelphia at Four Seasons Hotel Philadelphia, before joining The Surf Club Restaurant by Thomas Keller in Florida. Now, taking the helm at White Barn Inn, Auberge Collection, Sühr is translating years of classical training and global experience through the lens of coastal Maine, allowing the landscape and its changing seasons to dictate the menu. As autumn settles over Maine, the signature Coast Line & Forest tasting menu evolves to reflect the season, tracing a progression from the coastline to the deeper flavors of land, smoke, and fire. Drawing on Maine’s farms, waters, and forests, Sühr uses techniques including fermentation, preservation, smoking, and live-fire cooking to bring depth and character to ingredients at their peak. The menu continues to evolve with seasonal availability, allowing each harvest to shape the experience. Priced at $250 per guest, with an optional $125 wine pairing, the current menu features: Halibut | Razor Clams | Potato | Dill This dish captures the character of Maine’s coastline while incorporating the elegance of classical French cooking. The halibut offers natural sweetness and a delicate, flaky texture, while the razor clams bring subtle brininess and a slightly firmer bite. Potato adds an earthy, comforting element suited to the fall season, while dill provides freshness and a gentle aromatic lift. The sauce draws inspiration from traditional French moules marinières , using shellfish, white wine, and aromatics to create depth without detracting from the purity of the fish. The result strikes a balance between simplicity and refinement, bringing together familiar coastal New England ingredients through a delicate, contemporary interpretation of French technique that allows the natural flavors of the sea to remain the focus. Stonington Lobster | Parisian Gnocchi | Sea Beans | Fennel Sourcing lobster from Stonington, known as one of Maine’s premier lobster fishing towns, is particularly special. With its deeply rooted fishing heritage, the small coastal community represents much of what makes Maine’s culinary identity unique: tradition, craftsmanship, and a close connection to the sea. Stonington lobster is prized for its natural sweetness and beautiful texture, with succulent, tender meat that retains a delicate firmness and almost buttery richness. Parisian gnocchi introduces a light, airy texture that contrasts beautifully with the lobster, while sea beans bring a crisp bite and subtle ocean salinity. Fennel adds freshness and gentle anise notes. The sauce draws inspiration from a traditional Provençal bourride , lending silky, velvety richness that enhances the lobster’s natural sweetness without overpowering it. The dish brings together two coastal traditions: Stonington’s fishing heritage and the elegance of southern French cuisine. articles.title: Bar Prince Unveils Mythical Legends: A New Cocktail Menu Inspired By Scotland’s Most Enchanting Folklore
articles.titleKo: Bar Prince Unveils Mythical Legends: A New Cocktail Menu Inspired By Scotland’s Most Enchanting Folklore
articles.originalSummary: Following the success of last year’s Connected Icons , Bar Prince at The Balmoral invites guests into a world of myth, magic and storytelling with the launch of its newest cocktail menu, Mythical Legends . Launching this autumn, Mythical Legends draws inspiration from Scotland’s most enduring folklore, transforming legendary creatures and ancient tales into an immersive cocktail experience. From unicorns and selkies to witches, dragons and kelpies, the menu celebrates the stories that have captivated imaginations for generations. Overseen by Head Bartender Mattia Rovaris, each signature cocktail has been individually created by Bar Prince’s mixologists, with every serve inspired by a different Scottish legend. Guests are invited to discover the inspiration behind each creation, with every drink offering its own connection to Scotland’s rich mythical heritage. The theme extends beyond the cocktails themselves. Bespoke illustrations bring each character to life, transforming the menu into a contemporary storybook. Each copy has been meticulously handcrafted by Edinburgh’s Crawford Bookbinders, whose traditional techniques and attention to detail add another layer of craftsmanship, echoing Scotland’s long tradition of storytelling and artistry. Enhancing the experience further is a bespoke Mythical Legends Scent Mist, inspired by Scotland’s ancient forests, mist-covered lochs and legendary landscapes. Blending notes of cedarwood, chamomile and sandalwood with Scots pine, citrus and warming spice, it has been designed to transport guests into the world that inspired the cocktails. Capturing the spirit of Scotland’s wild landscapes and folklore through new techniques and evocative flavour combinations, highlights include The Untamed One , a shimmering tribute to Scotland’s national animal, the unicorn, blending Scottish vodka with coconut water, white chocolate, banana and lime leaf for an elegant serve. Double Identity , inspired by the selkie’s existence between land and sea, reimagines the whisky sour with coastal Scotch whisky, honey, citrus and warming spice. Meanwhile, Kingdom’s Cauldron draws on the tale of the Witch of Fife, combining whisky, botanicals, chocolate, vanilla and caramel into a rich and mysterious after-dark cocktail. Elsewhere, guests can discover the inspiration behind Messy-Nessie , a bright and herbaceous whisky highball inspired by Scotland’s most famous monster, or enjoy Fairy Queen , a decadent take on the Mai Tai featuring aged rum, roasted Brazil nuts and dark cacao. More than a cocktail menu, Mythical Legends is an invitation to explore Scotland’s legendary past through flavour, artistry and imagination. Continuing Bar Prince’s commitment to innovative cocktail storytelling, each drink reveals a new chapter in Scotland’s rich folklore. Mattia Rovaris, Head Bartender at Bar Prince, said: “Building on the success of Connected Icons, Mythical Legends gave our team the opportunity to tell a new chapter of Scotland’s story through the lens of folklore. Each cocktail has been created by a different member of the bar team, making the menu a true collective of ideas, creativity and personal interpretation. Paired with bespoke illustrations and scent, we’ve created an experience that invites guests to discover something new with every serve.” Discover the stories, flavours and aromas behind Scotland’s most captivating folklore at Bar Prince at The Balmoral. Mythical Legends launches this autumn. For more information or to reserve a table, visit: https://www.roccofortehotels.com/hotels-and-resorts/the-balmoral-hotel/dining/bar-prince/cocktail-menu/

articles.titleKo: How P.F. Chang’s Alexa Bunting Turned Customer Curiosity into Brand Storytelling
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Alexa Bunting’s career began in sales at fine jewelry retailers, where she grew curious about the psychology behind why customers buy. That curiosity sent her back to school for a master’s degree in integrated marketing. Her first taste of food and beverage marketing came at Black Rifle Coffee Co., where she led marketing for the brand’s retail coffee shops. She dove headfirst into a fast-moving environment with a constant rotation of new beverages, new menu items, and seasonal flair to promote. But her biggest takeaway was how to build a community and tell a story. “I learned the importance of building a community around your brand,” Bunting says. “Black Rifle has a strong customer base, and I learned pretty quickly that although sales and discounts drive consumers in, it’s the brand that keeps them coming back.” Today, Bunting is the director of brand marketing at P.F. Chang’s. “That’s what I’ve carried through to P.F. Chang’s,” she says. “The question here is, how do we build something that goes beyond our food? How do we create a community and that emotional storytelling component that keeps people coming back and supporting us? Those little moments where you can be involved with your community make your marketing so much stronger, and your brand so much stronger.” There, she approaches marketing as a sequence: It starts with a strong menu, followed by a compelling story that draws guests in, then operational execution and interactive touches in the dining room. It’s a fully integrated approach that spans every channel, but it all starts with the brief. Join women leaders at WiRL! Reserve your spot today. That approach is part of a broader resurgence at P.F. Chang’s . Under CEO Jim Mazany and chief marketing officer Holly Smith, who joined in January, the chain posted a 7.7 percent same-store sales gain in the second quarter, with traffic up 6.8 percent. “Holly and I sat down and thought to ourselves: How do we create something that’s uniquely ownable to P.F. Chang’s?” Bunting says. “How do we tie it back to something culturally relevant that only we can own?” Working with brand manager Olivia Liu, the team built 2026 around a series of seasonal campaigns inspired by Japanese culture. It started in February with Flavor In Bloom , a nod to Japan’s cherry blossom season that paired best-sellers like Chang’s Lettuce Wraps with spring cocktails, led by a Cherry Blossom Martini. Summer brought the city lights and street culture of Tokyo with Summer in Tokyo , which combined a new seasonal menu with the debut of the Sushi Boat, a shareable platter that arrives tableside in a cloud of dry ice. “At the heart of every campaign we’re doing, we give the consumers an educational element or a story that will pull it all together for them,” Bunting says. “We’ve really started to color a little outside of the lines with our LTOs and integrate them with things that are P.F. Chang’s at its core.” For fall, the brand turned to Kyoto. With Autumn in Kyoto , it added duck to the menu for a deeper, cozier experience inspired by one of Japan’s most celebrated seasons. Maple appears on the menu, including in the bourbon-based Kyoto Cabin cocktail, and throughout the campaign’s fall-inspired design. “In the spring, we centered around the Japanese cherry blossom, and what we realized after our research is that the maple tree is the twin flame to this during the fall in Japanese culture, so we really channeled that for this campaign,” she says. articles.title: Bread Zeppelin Announces $2 Discount on Chicken Caesar Zeppelin Combo
articles.titleKo: Bread Zeppelin Announces $2 Discount on Chicken Caesar Zeppelin Combo
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . While other sandwich chains are introducing scaled-down options to reach a lower price, Bread Zeppelin is keeping its Chicken Caesar combo exactly the size guests know and charging less for it. From Oct. 21-28, guests at participating Dallas-Fort Worth locations can get the Chicken Caesar Zeppelin combo for $2 less than the usual $9.99. The promotion follows the Oct. 12 rollout of Jersey Mike’s $7.99 Mini Bundle , which features a smaller cold sub and a bag of chips. Bread Zeppelin is matching that price and upping the protein — its Caesar packs 41 grams, roughly 128% more than the 18-gram minimum Jersey Mike’s reports for those sandwiches. “I’m a Jersey Mike’s fan. I’ve got the rewards account to prove it,” said co-founder Troy Charhon. “But I’ll put our deal up against theirs any day. We know many of our neighbors are being more mindful of how they spend their hard-earned money. We want to give them something they can feel good about choosing, without having to compromise on quality or value.” The build features their full-sized toasted baguette, cored out and loaded with romaine, Parmesan, Caesar dressing and chicken marinated and grilled in-house, never frozen — also available as a salad bowl. Even the croutons have a backstory. They’re housemade from the bread cores pulled during prep, so nothing goes to waste. “When we sat down to put this offer together, making the Zeppelin smaller never even came up,” said co-founder Andrew Schoellkopf. “Same delicious baguette, same grilled chicken, same 41 grams of protein. We’d rather just charge less for it and let our guests taste for themselves what all the hype is about.” For more information or to view the menu, visit breadzeppelin.com or follow @breadzeppelin on social media. *While supplies last. Additional restrictions may apply. Available for dine-in, take-out and in app purchases only, no third party orders accepted. articles.title: KNEAD Hospitality + Design Names Juan Pablo Loza Culinary Director of Mi Vida
articles.titleKo: KNEAD Hospitality + Design Names Juan Pablo Loza Culinary Director of Mi Vida
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . KNEAD Hospitality + Design has announced that Chef Juan Pablo Loza has joined Mi Vida as Culinary Director. This is the first menu change of its kind for both KNEAD and Mi Vida since opening in 2018 as the group continues its ongoing market expansion with locations across Washington, D.C., Philadelphia, and Virginia Beach. The exciting new chapter is a culmination of seven years of a professional relationship and friendship with KNEAD Hospitality + Design co-principals, Jason Berry and Michael Reginbogin, who first connected with Loza during his tenure at Rosewood Mayakoba. “We’ve known Chef Juan Pablo for many years and have always admired his approach to cooking and hospitality,” said Berry. “We’ve had the opportunity to watch his career evolve since we first met him at Rosewood Mayakoba, so having him lead the next chapter of Mi Vida’s culinary direction feels like a very natural fit.” Loza grew up in Mexico City’s Xochimilco neighborhood, spending afternoons at the local market with his mother and grandmother cleaning beans and prepping tomatillos. He began training at 16 under French chef Olivier Lombard, followed by four years in the high-pressure kitchen of Mexico City’s Lasser. He went on to win the Guillermo Ríos Young Mexican Chef Competition, a national competition hosted by Ambrosia Centro Culinario and judged by chefs including Enrique Olvera and Ricardo Muñoz Zurita. After culinary positions at Le Cirque, Ciboulette and L’Olivier, Loza built an international hospitality career with Rosewood Hotels & Resorts, Belmond and Auberge Resorts Collection across Mexico, the Caribbean and South America. He spent eight years as Executive Chef and Director of Culinary Operations at Rosewood Mayakoba, overseeing six restaurants and bars—including Zapote Bar, ranked No. 11 on North America’s 50 Best Bars in 2023 and 2024—and transforming a beach food truck he launched into the $8 million Aqui Me Quedo beach club. Most recently, he served as Director of Culinary Experiences at Chileno Bay Resort & Residences before opening Señora Cocina, Casa & Cantina in San José del Cabo in March 2025. His extensive experience across international luxury resort markets gives him a unique perspective on bridging American diners’ tastes with authentic, regional Mexican flavors and ingredients. Loza will bring what he calls his own version of Mexico to the Mi Vida menu – lighter, brighter cooking built on vegetables, acidity, and technique. His approach challenges misconceptions that Mexican cooking is “heavy” by highlighting its fresh, vibrant nature. He’s rebalancing the menu’s traditional weight, turning some of Mi Vida’s richer dishes into starters while building new main courses designed to feel lighter without sacrificing flavor: a chile-rubbed salmon over avocado-citrus purée with a cucumber and preserved lemon salad; ribs reimagined through the lens of tacos al pastor, finished with charred pineapple and cured onion; a crispy pork shank recast as carnitas alongside a bright, citrus-lifted salsa verde; and a banana leaf-wrapped barbacoa short rib served with a chilled, chickpea salad for contrast. A guacamole built with grasshoppers and chorizo, “Guacamole Oaxaca,” reflects his belief that trying something unfamiliar is part of what makes dining out worth it. Mi Vida, Spanish for “my life,” is a fitting name for what Loza calls deeply personal cooking. By merging his culinary vision with KNEAD’s signature design, Loza is looking forward to being a part of DC’s thriving culinary scene. “Cooking has always been a deeply personal expression of who I am, where I come from, and the experiences that have shaped me,” said Loza. “I’m excited to bring my perspective to Mi Vida, while honoring the cuisine I grew up eating. articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . The Olo app launches on Tuesday. More than two decades after Noah Glass first envisioned a digital network connecting restaurants and their customers, the Olo founder and CEO is preparing to bring that idea directly to consumers. On Tuesday, Olo will launch its namesake mobile app, giving customers a single destination to order pickup and delivery from restaurants across its network. The platform introduces what Glass calls “second-party” ordering, a model that combines the convenience of third-party marketplaces with the economics and customer relationships associated with restaurants’ direct ordering channels. The proposition is straightforward. Customers can browse multiple brands without paying inflated menu prices, and operators receive the full profit from each order without marketplace commissions. Olo, meanwhile, collects a 5 percent fee from consumers. The launch represents a significant expansion of Olo’s business, taking a company known primarily as a behind-the-scenes technology provider into a consumer-facing market dominated by DoorDash and Uber Eats. Glass says the concept dates to an executive summary he wrote in December 2003, years before Olo became an established restaurant technology provider. “To say that this is like a nearly 23-year dream come true this launch Tuesday is not hyperbole,” Glass says. Olo’s acquisition by private equity firm Thoma Bravo helped accelerate the initiative. Glass says the shift from a publicly traded software provider to a privately owned company created greater flexibility to pursue a network business model. His conviction was significant enough that he and his family reinvested 75 percent of their transaction proceeds into Olo. The immediate opportunity lies in addressing longstanding friction in restaurant digital ordering. Individual restaurant apps can be expensive to acquire customers for and difficult to sustain engagement with. Third-party marketplaces offer considerable consumer reach, but restaurants sacrifice margins through commissions, advertising expenses, and limited access to customer information. Olo believes there is an underserved audience between dedicated restaurantttt loyalists and consumers committed to subscription programs such as DashPass and Uber One. “There’s a big group in the middle, I would argue, and probably the majority of the overall population that wants the convenience of being able to order from many different brands in one place,” Glass says. Glass doesn’t view the app primarily as a vehicle to shift existing transactions away from restaurant-owned channels. He expects the lower cost of ordering to encourage additional occasions among consumers who have become discouraged by delivery prices. The potential savings are a significant component of Olo’s consumer pitch. Glass says menu markups on traditional marketplaces frequently range from 15 to 30 percent, adding costs that customers may mistakenly attribute to restaurants. He points to an $85 delivery order he recently placed through the Olo app that cost $19.34 less than the equivalent marketplace transaction, even after Olo’s 5 percent fee. The platform will disclose that fee during checkout and inform customers that ordering directly from a restaurant is the least expensive option. Delivery fees and tips still apply when customers choose delivery, but Olo avoids the additional menu markups that can make marketplace orders considerably more expensive. Another advantage is that Olo isn’t starting its consumer network from scratch. Impeccable announced that co-founder Carlos Boozer has taken on the full-time role of chief growth officer, expanding his involvement with the vertically integrated real estate and restaurant platform as it continues to grow throughout the Southeast. In his new role, Boozer will work across Impeccable Capital’s diverse portfolio, including Impeccable Development and Impeccable Restaurant Group, to strengthen the companies’ public presence, build strategic relationships and identify new business opportunities. He will also participate in executive planning and work directly with leaders across Impeccable’s investment, development and restaurant businesses. “Carlos has been an integral part of Impeccable from the beginning,” said Rob Tanner, founder and CEO of Impeccable. “He has an extraordinary ability to connect with people and see opportunity across industries. We want that perspective involved as we grow our existing businesses and explore what comes next.” “I helped build Impeccable because I believed in what we could create together,” Boozer said. “I’m excited to take a bigger role in the day-to-day business, spending time with our teams, showing up in the communities we serve and bringing the right people together to help us grow.” As chief growth officer, Boozer will help drive Impeccable’s growth by using his visibility, credibility and relationships to open doors to investors, strategic partners and new business opportunities. Working closely with CEO Rob Tanner and the company’s leadership team, he will build key relationships, make qualified introductions and evaluate potential new lines of business. Boozer will represent Impeccable at conferences, speaking engagements, media appearances, investor meetings and company events, including restaurant openings. He will also visit restaurants and development projects, strengthen connections with employees, franchise brands and community leaders, and participate in executive planning to help turn promising opportunities into long-term growth. A two-time NBA All-Star and Olympic gold medalist, Boozer played 13 seasons in the NBA for the Cleveland Cavaliers, Utah Jazz, Chicago Bulls and Los Angeles Lakers. He represented the United States at the 2004 and 2008 Olympic Games, winning bronze in Athens and gold in Beijing. The 2008 U.S. Olympic men’s basketball team, known as the “Redeem Team,” was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame as part of its class of 2025. Since retiring from professional basketball, Boozer has focused on entrepreneurship, franchising and commercial real estate. As a co-founder and investor in Impeccable Capital, Impeccable Development and Impeccable Restaurant Group, he also serves on Impeccable Development’s board of directors and real estate committee. Boozer’s expanded role comes as Impeccable continues to scale its real estate development and restaurant operations throughout the Southeast. Impeccable Development has more than 25 active projects, with approximately 2 million square feet developed or under development. The company specializes in ground-up retail, restaurant and select mixed-use developments, working with national and regional brands throughout its portfolio. articles.title: What the Meritage Chapter 11 Teaches Restaurant Franchisees
articles.titleKo: What the Meritage Chapter 11 Teaches Restaurant Franchisees
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Meritage shows that a single day can decide whether a debtor has hundreds of restaurants to reorganize or none at all. One day after Wendy’s cut it loose, the operator of 314 Wendy’s-franchised restaurants filed for bankruptcy to keep its franchises alive. The case tests a question many distressed franchisees face: Can bankruptcy save a franchise the franchisor says is already gone? Timing and venue are critical. Quality Is Our Recipe, LLC (“QIOR”), a Wendy’s subsidiary, notified Meritage Hospitality Group on Sept. 16, 2026, that all its franchise agreements were terminated “effective immediately.” Meritage, which operates 314 franchised restaurants in 15 states, filed chapter 11 the next day in the Western District of Michigan to stay termination. In re Meritage Hospitality Group Inc. , No. 26-02947 (Bankr. W.D. Mich.). QIOR claims roughly $146.9 million, including $119.5 million in “continuous operations fees.” The Adversary Proceeding On October 1, 2026, the debtors sued QIOR and Wendy’s seeking declaratory relief that the termination was ineffective, the franchise agreements are estate property and the automatic stay bars enforcement. The dispute traces to an October 2025 payment-default notice and three forbearance letters, the last expiring August 18, 2026. QIOR’s emailed termination notice demanded more than $146 million by Oct. 16, 2026, and tendered a short-term license agreement (“STLA”) through year-end. The debtors allege the termination failed because the agreements required physical (not email) notice; QIOR did not give lenders the required notice and cure opportunity under the consents to collateral assignment; cure periods restarted upon forbearance expiration; and the STLA and QIOR’s reserved purchase option presupposed a continuing relationship. Can Chapter 11 Resurrect a Terminated Franchise Agreement? The answer turns on timing. A franchise agreement not fully terminated at filing becomes estate property under 11 U.S.C. § 541, and the automatic stay (§ 362(a)) bars termination without stay relief. See In re Welcome Group 2, LLC , 660 B.R. 874, 879 (Bankr. S.D. Ohio 2024); In re Mirant Corp. , 440 F.3d 238, 252–53 (5th Cir. 2006). Conversely, contracts that have expired or were validly terminated prior to bankruptcy leave the debtor “with nothing to assume or reject.” In re P.I.N.E., Inc. , 52 B.R. 463, 465 (Bankr. W.D. Mich. 1985). QIOR and Wendy’s respond that the agreements “have been terminated” and are not estate property. Meritage argues that even a valid termination leaves residual interests, including the right to seek reinstatement. Meritage’s fight turns on whether the Sept. 16 notice completed the job or merely started a process interrupted by the stay. The notice reserved QIOR’s options to buy equipment and take over leases, obligations Meritage calls “diametrically inconsistent” with a completed termination. The default notice set state-specific cure periods of 90, 60 and 30 days, later deferred by forbearance, inviting arguments that fresh notice was required. The interim license offer arguably belies a clean break. And the lender-notice argument may prove decisive; QIOR admits the consent language but pleads compliance. Notably, a bare right to terminate may not itself establish “cause” for stay relief under § 362(d)(1). See Mirant , 440 F.3d at 253. Meritage’s Restructuring Strategy and Operations Meritage operates as a debtor in possession, with a strategy of closing or selling underperforming stores, resolving the QIOR dispute, potential market sales and a recapitalization. articles.title: New York–Style Pizzeria Barsella to Open Near SMU’s Campus
articles.titleKo: New York–Style Pizzeria Barsella to Open Near SMU’s Campus
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . A new locally-owned restaurant and bar is coming to SMU Boulevard this winter. Barsella, an Italian-American restaurant, New York-style pizzeria and cocktail bar, will open at 5600 SMU Blvd., Suite 120 in Dallas for dinner and late night, with slices from a walk-up window during the day. Barsella is the first hospitality concept from Dallas native Oliver Steinberg. Barsella is meant to work for more than one kind of night. Guests can settle in for dinner and a bottle of wine, meet friends for happy hour, grab a New York-style slice from the window, enjoy spritzes on the patio or end the evening with drinks and late-night bites. “Barsella was designed in hopes of becoming a neighborhood institution, elevated enough for a great dinner or date night, approachable enough to become your regular spot, and lively enough to be where you want to end the night,” says Dallas resident and creator of the concept, Oliver Steinberg. “We wanted to create a place where families, couples, friends and neighbors all feel equally at home, whatever brings them in that night,” he adds. From the dining room to the slice window, each space has its own identity and energy, all served by the same kitchen and consistent approach to food and hospitality. At its core, the new restaurant offers a thoughtful take on Italian-American dining. “The menu is intentionally filled with dishes people know, love and want to order such as rigatoni alla vodka, ravioli and lasagna, yet executed at a high level,” expresses Steinberg. Many dishes take inspiration from iconic New York pizzerias and restaurants the culinary team visited while developing the menu. The goal is food that is craveable and memorable without ever feeling overly complicated or intimidating, paired with an extensive spritz and craft cocktail program and a thoughtfully developed wine list. New York-style pizza isn’t an accessory to the bar or dining room; it is one of the foundations of the concept. Inside, a seven-seat pizza bar offers a more casual way to experience the restaurant, sharing the slice window’s menu along with offerings beyond pizza. Walking up to the slice window is meant to feel like stepping beneath the marquee of a Broadway theater, with bright, theatrical signage recognizable from down the street. The window serves individual slices from a mix of staple pies and rotating specials. The patio, envisioned as a bit of an Italian escape with a pergola and lemon-vine plantings overhead, is a natural place to enjoy one, and large sliding windows connect it to the interior bar. As dinner fades into night, Barsella becomes a late-night spritz and cocktail bar. Live music fills the room most Thursday through Saturday nights, and a dedicated menu of light bites, featuring dishes guests won’t find everywhere else, is served until 2 a.m. An intimate private dining room of approximately 16 seats can also host private dinners, celebrations and events, carrying the same green tones, tile and millwork throughout. Liz Johnson of Wallace Johnson Studio is leading the interior design, drawing on classic Italian-American concepts, New York cafés and European aperitivo culture for a space that feels polished, bright and colorful rather than dark and rustic. Hexagonal mosaic floors, olive-green millwork, green tile and red pleated booths set the tone inside the approximately 3,100-square-foot space which will seat 80 in the main dining room. Barsella is slated to open this winter at 5600 SMU Blvd., Suite 120, Dallas, Texas. Additional details on the menu and opening date will be announced closer to opening. articles.title: Hangry Joe’s New CEO Wants to Build a Better Franchise System, Not Just a Bigger One
articles.titleKo: Hangry Joe’s New CEO Wants to Build a Better Franchise System, Not Just a Bigger One
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Brandon Wihelm was named Hangry Joe's CEO in early October. Brandon Wilhelm wasn’t necessarily looking to take on another major role in the restaurant industry. After spending nearly two decades developing Subway franchise territory across the Midwest, he was considering opportunities outside the business. Then he discovered Hangry Joe’s. Wilhelm traveled to Virginia to explore the emerging hot chicken concept, arriving a day early to secretly visit several restaurants before meeting with the corporate team. He came away impressed with the food, but also saw opportunities to improve the young franchise’s marketing, real estate strategy, and operational infrastructure. That combination eventually led him to become a multi-unit franchisee, equity investor, board member, and, as of October 6, CEO of the growing fast-casual chain. “I went out to Virginia and and tried the food and checked out the brand and it was the best chicken sandwich I ever had,” Wilhelm says. Founded in 2021, Hangry Joe’s has expanded to more than 90 restaurants across over 20 states and international markets, including the United Arab Emirates. Another 20 locations are in the pipeline. But Wilhelm isn’t measuring the company’s future success solely through restaurant count. His immediate priority is creating a more profitable, sustainable franchise system that can support expansion without repeating some of the mistakes that accompanied its early growth. His experience includes overseeing operations strategy for more than 500 Subway restaurants and working with more than 140 franchisees. He also served as president of Hangry Development Texas and acting chief marketing officer of Hangry Joe’s. Those experiences informed a series of proposals he presented to the company’s founders and board over the past year. The discussions eventually resulted in an invitation to implement the plans himself. “I have no real desire to say, ‘OK, we’re going to grow this to a certain level and then we’re going to sell it to private equity.’ That’s never been my goal, and I’ve told those guys from the beginning,” Wilhelm says. Wilhelm’s initial priorities include reducing food costs, improving purchasing efficiency, increasing consumer awareness, and establishing more rigorous development standards. Supply chain improvements represent one of the most immediate opportunities. Historically, individual franchisees have had considerable flexibility in sourcing certain products, creating inconsistencies that can limit the company’s purchasing power. Wilhelm wants greater compliance with approved distribution relationships to negotiate more favorable pricing across the system. The company is also examining freight expenses, including proprietary ingredients that some operators currently purchase by the pallet and ship directly to individual restaurants. Consolidating those purchases through distribution facilities could eliminate unnecessary expenses and make inventory replenishment more efficient. Additional opportunities include renegotiating vendor agreements and examining third-party delivery commission rates. The challenge is lowering expenses without changing the ingredients and preparation methods that distinguish Hangry Joe’s from competitors. “Our product and our process and all that kind of stuff is not going to change,” Wilhelm says. “Our proprietary seasonings, our proprietary marinade, and the quality of chicken that we get in, none of that’s going to change.” The same attention to unit economics is influencing Hangry Joe’s development strategy.
